detail.title: Adaptive Social Behavior Inventory (ASBI)
detail.introduction: The Adaptive Social Behavior Inventory (ASBI) is a caregiver- and teacher-reported measure designed to assess young children’s social competence in early childhood. It was developed to capture social skills as a multidimensional construct that is conceptually distinct from social pathology or behavior problems. The ASBI consists of 30 items organised into three subscales—Express, Comply, and Disrupt—reflecting children’s ability to express positive social behaviours, comply with social rules and expectations, and manage disruptive or problematic behaviours. The measure can be completed by adults who know the child well in everyday contexts, including parents or early years practitioners, and is intended for use with children in the preschool period.

measures.name: ADHD rating scale – 5 for Children and Adolescents

detail.title: ADHD rating scale – 5 for Children and Adolescents
detail.introduction: The ADHD Rating Scale–5 (ADHD-RS-5) is an 18-item screening assessment completed by parents and teachers to measure ADHD symptoms in children and adolescents in line with DSM-5 diagnostic criteria. The scale includes two subscales—Inattention and Hyperactivity/Impulsivity—and assesses six areas of impairment: relationships, peer interactions, academics, behavior, homework, and self-esteem.The measure is available in separate child (ages 5–10) and adolescent (ages 11–17) versions, with developmentally appropriate symptom descriptions. Items are rated on a 4-point Likert scale reflecting symptom frequency, with separate forms for home and school settings. Each form takes approximately 5 minutes to complete, and complete instructions are provided for scoring and interpretation, including separate scoring profiles for symptoms and impairments for boys and girls.

detail.title: ADHD Symptom Checklist‑4
detail.introduction: The ADHD Symptom Checklist-4 (ADHD-SC4) is a 50-item screening rating scale used to evaluate response to treatment for symptoms of AD/HD and Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) in children and adolescents aged 3 to 18 years. A single version of the measure can be completed by both parents and teachers.The ADHD-SC4 comprises four subscales: DSM-5 symptoms of AD/HD; DSM-5 symptoms of ODD; the Peer Conflict Scale, which assesses interpersonal peer aggression; and the Stimulant Side Effects Checklist, used to monitor medication effects. The checklist takes approximately 5 minutes to complete and is designed to be quick and easy to score.

detail.title: Ages & Stages Questionnaires (ASQ‑3)
detail.introduction: The Ages & Stages Questionnaires®, Third Edition (ASQ®-3) is a developmental screening tool that pinpoints developmental progress in children between the ages of one month to 5 ½ years. Its success lies in its parent-centric approach and inherent ease-of-use—a combination that has made it the most widely used developmental screener across the globe. Evidence shows that the earlier development is assessed—the greater the chance a child has to reach his or her potential

fields.label: Prior qualifications/training required
fields.value: No formal professional qualifications are required for completion because ASQ‑3 is completed by parents or primary caregivers. However, interpretation and referral decisions are typically made by health professionals such as pediatricians or health visitors.

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: Easy. Scoring is rule-based and straightforward. Item scores are summed within each domain and compared to fixed cut-off thresholds defined at two standard deviations below the normative mean to classify children as above cut-off, close to cut-off, or below cut-off.

fields.label: Floor effects
fields.value: In the ParentChild+ evaluation, the authors report that many children scored near the upper end of several ASQ‑3 domains, indicating ceiling effects and reduced score variation.

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: 226,505 children. The study used secondary data from England’s Community Service datased (CSDS). They show how the sample compares to national data.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The ASQ‑3 was used as a parent-reported secondary outcome measure in the ParentChild+ and Maths Champions evaluations to assess children’s early developmental functioning. It was administered to parents of children aged approximately 2 – 4 years. The ASQ‑3 measures development across five domains: Communication, Gross Motor, Fine Motor, Problem Solving, and Personal-Social. In the Peep Learning Together evaluation, ASQ‑3 was used as part of the wider assessment battery to capture broader developmental outcomes alongside language and early literacy.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the ParentChild+ evaluation, the authors report that many children scored near the upper end of several ASQ‑3 domains, indicating ceiling effects and reduced score variation.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: No structural adaptations were made to the ASQ‑3 instrument itself. Across trials, the ASQ‑3 was completed by parents rather than practitioners, and in ParentChild+, some assessments were completed online due to COVID-19 restrictions rather than face-to-face. In analysis, ceiling effects required cautious interpretation, particularly in domains where most children scored at the upper limits of the scale.

The ASQ‑3 was used as a parent-reported secondary outcome measure in the ParentChild+ and Maths Champions evaluations to assess children’s early developmental functioning. It was administered to parents of children aged approximately 2 – 4 years. The ASQ‑3 measures development across five domains: Communication, Gross Motor, Fine Motor, Problem Solving, and Personal-Social. In the Peep Learning Together evaluation, ASQ‑3 was used as part of the wider assessment battery to capture broader developmental outcomes alongside language and early literacy.

Key Learnings
In the ParentChild+ evaluation, the authors report that many children scored near the upper end of several ASQ‑3 domains, indicating ceiling effects and reduced score variation.

Adaptations made
No structural adaptations were made to the ASQ‑3 instrument itself. Across trials, the ASQ‑3 was completed by parents rather than practitioners, and in ParentChild+, some assessments were completed online due to COVID-19 restrictions rather than face-to-face. In analysis, ceiling effects required cautious interpretation, particularly in domains where most children scored at the upper limits of the scale.

detail.title: Ainsworth Maternal Sensitivity Scale (AMSS)
detail.introduction: The Ainsworth Maternal Sensitivity Scale is used to measure the sensitivity of the mother of children aged 3 to 24 months (or thereabouts). The tool measures the mother's ability to perceive the infant's signals accurately and to respond to these signals promptly and appropriately. A score is generated on a 9-point scale (9 = high, 1 = low) for a number of important maternal traits. The scores are generated by observing the interaction between the mother and infant in a variety of settings (that is, play, feeding, teaching). It may be conducted in the home or the laboratory, and has been used to assess the sensitivity of fathers and mothers in non-Western populations. It is reported to take from 25 minutes up to 2 hours and is freely available.

detail.title: Assessment for Persons With Profound or Severe Impairments (APPSI‑2)
detail.introduction: The APPSI-2 is an easy-to-administer test built specifically for clinicians working with clients of any age who are preverbal and functioning at a mental age of 0 to 24 months. The test’s second edition has been fully reconceptualized to create an assessment system that is comprehensive enough to aid in planning effective individualized instruction for these examinees. Results can be used to (a) identify abilities and behaviors that clients are able to demonstrate, (b) plan effective intervention, and (c) monitor progress in mastery of new abilities. The APPSI-2 also aids in defining an individual’s preferred methods of communication, which is most useful for planning instruction to enhance his or her independence.

We selected institutions of early childhood education located in each district and county via convenience sampling. We then asked for their voluntary participation. Thirteen institutions consented to participate after we explained the purpose, content, and procedures of this study to the head of the institution and teachers. 322 consent forms were signed and returned by parents. The study was conducted on all children who agreed to participate; however, 36 children who presented a language delay in the Preschool Language Receptive and Expressive Language Scale (PRES) test were excluded from the overall data. This left us with 286 participants for the final analysis — 145 boys (50.7%) and 141 girls (49.3%). They were 76.12-months-old on average (SD = 3.51).

Participants were six-year-old children attending Korean kindergartens and nurseries located in a metropolitan city in Korea. Thirteen institutions consented to participate after we explained the purpose, content, and procedures of this study to the head of the institution and teachers. 322 consent forms were signed and returned by parents. detail.title: Attention Network test [ANT]
detail.introduction: The ANT is a task designed to test three attentional networks in children and adults: alerting, orienting, and executive control. Efficiency of the alerting network is examined by changes in reaction time resulting from a warning signal. Efficiency of orienting is examined by changes in the reaction time that accompany cues indicating where the target will occur. The efficiency of the executive network is examined by requiring the participant to respond by pressing two keys indicating the direction (left or right) of a central arrow surrounded by congruent, incongruent or neutral flankers.

detail.title: Bankson-Bernthal Test of Phonology – Second Edition (BBTOP‑2)
detail.introduction: The Bankson-Bernthal Test of Phonology–Second Edition (BBTOP-2) is an individually administered assessment of young children’s speech-sound development. The test is actually three assessments in one: a whole-word accuracy analysis, an inventory of consonant articulation, and an assessment of common phonological error patterns. Colorful illustrations are used to elicit the child’s pronunciation of 80 common stimulus words. To administer the BBTOP-2, the examiner simply points to each illustration and has the child name it. The stimulus words are conveniently preprinted in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) on the record form. The examiner uses IPA to transcribe any words the child misarticulates. After the child has named all 80 stimulus words and test administration has concluded, the examiner uses the transcription of the misarticulated words to complete the Consonant Articulation Inventory, which assesses articulation of both initial and final consonants. Finally, the examiner can complete the Error Pattern Assessment of common phonological error patterns that may be evident in the misarticulated words. The test’s results can be used to (a) identify children who have speech-sound disorders, (b) plan interventions, and (c) represent speech-sound development and speech-sound disorders in research studies.

detail.introduction: The Battelle® Developmental Inventory, Third Edition (BDI-3®) is a research-backed, IDEA-aligned tool for assessing children from birth through age 7 years, 11 months. detail.title: Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Develpoment 4 (BSID)
detail.introduction: The Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development (BSID) is designed to assess and/or monitor very young children at risk of developmental delays or disorders. It provides an indication of the child's current developmental level and can also offer a cautious prognosis regarding expected development.

Most clinical, school, pediatric, counseling, neuro‑, and applied developmental psychologists have received such training. Administration and scoring of the various BASC – 3 components may, with appropriate training and supervision, be completed by clerical staff. Individuals who use the BASC – 3 with specialized populations (e.g., sensory impaired or recent immigrants from nonwestern cultures) are expected to have specialized training and experience in the use of such assessment devices and intervention materials with these populations. Sample controlled for Sex Race/ethnicity Geographic region SES/parent’s education Community size Inclusion of children from special education classifications . detail.title: Behavioural and Emotional Rating Scale (BERS‑3)
detail.introduction: The (BERS-3) Behavioral and Emotional Rating Scale – Third Edition is a multimodal assessment system that measures the behavior from three perspectives: the student (Youth Rating Scale), parent (Parent Rating Scale), and teacher or other professional (Teacher Rating Scale). The BERS-3 measures several aspects of student strengths: Interpersonal Strength, Family Involvement, Intrapersonal Strength, School Functioning, and Affective Strength. The subscales are useful in evaluating students for prereferral services, in placing students for specialized services, and in measuring the outcome of services. The BERS-3 can identify students’ individual behavior and emotional strengths and the areas in which educational strengths need to be developed.

detail.introduction: The Behavioral Observation of Students in Schools (BOSS) is an observation-based system for coding classroom behavior. BOSS is also useful for measuring ADHD symptoms as it has been shown to differentiate between children with ADHD and typically developing children. BOSS allows systematic recording of children's behaviors in the following domains: active engaged time, passive engagement time, off-task motor activity, off-task verbal behavior, off-task passive behaviors, and teacher-directed instruction.

detail.title: Boxall Profile
detail.introduction: This evidence-based tool from Nurture UK guides school settings through an in-depth wellbeing measurement to monitor student wellbeing.The tool aims to assist with identifying where additional support may be needed, set targets and track progress.It encourages a graduated approach to nurture, a concept which highlights the importance of social environments and its influence on social emotional skills, wellbeing and behaviour.The two-part checklist should be completed by a member of staff who knows the student very well. As well as identifying need, it provides a detailed assessment to help decide next steps to support student mental wellbeing.

detail.title: Brief Early Skills and Support Index (BESSI)
detail.introduction: The Brief Early Skills & Support Index (BESSI) is a brief teacher-report screening tool developed and validated for nursery and reception-aged children. It screens children’s early skills and support needs across social, emotional, cognitive, and daily functioning domains, with the aim of informing school readiness and early intervention.

fields.label: Prior qualifications/training required
fields.value: The BESSI was designed for use by classroom teachers and early years practitioners and does not require formal clinical or specialist qualifications.

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: Easy. Scoring involves summing item responses within each of the four domains to generate domain scores. The scoring process is straightforward and requires no specialized training.

fields.label: Floor effects
fields.value: In the PACT evaluation, the authors report that BESSI was used primarily as a secondary outcome measure and showed limited score variation. In the Peep Learning Together EYPP subgroup analysis, the authors similarly report limited variation in BESSI scores, affecting the extent to which change could be examined.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The BESSI was used in both the PACT and Peep Learning Together evaluations as a teacher-reported secondary outcome measure of children’s early behavioural adjustment and school readiness. It was administered to nursery and reception-aged children (ages 3 – 5) at baseline and follow-up. In the Peep evaluation, analysis focused primarily on the Behavioural Adjustment subscale as the key social-emotional outcome.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the PACT evaluation, the authors report that BESSI was used primarily as a secondary outcome measure and showed limited score variation. In the Peep Learning Together EYPP subgroup analysis, the authors similarly report limited variation in BESSI scores, affecting the extent to which change could be examined.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: No structural adaptations were made to the BESSI instrument itself. However, in the Peep trial, only the Behavioural Adjustment subscale was analysed as the primary social-emotional outcome rather than the full BESSI profile. In both trials, BESSI was completed by school staff familiar with the child, and administration occurred within routine school data collection processes, rather than under researcher-led testing conditions.

fields.value: Hughes, C., Daly, I., Foley, S., White, N. and Devine, R.T., 2015. Measuring the foundations of school readiness: Introducing a new questionnaire for teachers–The Brief Early Skills and Support Index (BESSI). British Journal of Educational Psychology, 85(3), pp.332-356.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: CELF was used as a standardised outcome measure of early language development across multiple EEF-funded early years trials. In the URLEY programme, CELF formed part of a composite language outcome alongside BPVS and Renfrew measures to assess language development in nursery and reception children aged 3 – 5. In EasyPeasy, CELF Preschool 2 UK was used as the primary outcome measure to evaluate the impact of a 20-week parent-delivered play-based intervention with children aged 3 – 4. CELF was also used in NELI as part of a battery of four language tests to measure receptive and expressive language in Reception pupils aged 4 – 5. In contrast, the PACT evaluation initially intended to use language assessments aligned with CELF-type constructs, but due to COVID-19 disruption, the primary language outcome was replaced with LanguageScreen, meaning CELF was not used at post-test. In Peep Learning Together, CELF-type standardised language testing was used as the primary outcome for core language skills in children aged 3 – 4, alongside early literacy as a secondary outcome.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the Nuffield Early Language Intervention (NELI) evaluation, the authors report that CELF subtests were administered only at post-test and were incorporated into a composite language outcome, rather than analysed individually. The evaluation notes that the absence of baseline CELF data meant that CELF could not be used to examine pre – post change directly and instead contributed to post-intervention and composite analyses.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: Across trials, CELF itself was not structurally adapted, but administration and outcome use were affected by delivery constraints, particularly COVID-19. In PACT, CELF was removed from post-testing entirely and replaced with LanguageScreen, with assessments delivered by school staff instead of blinded researchers. In EasyPeasy, CELF administration was completed as planned but only selected subscales were emphasised in reporting. In URLEY, CELF contributed to a composite outcome rather than being analysed as a standalone primary measure. In NELI, CELF-type outcomes were used alongside digital language screening rather than as the sole primary outcome. In Peep, CELF-informed language testing proceeded as planned, but 20% post-test attrition affected the final analytical sample.

detail.title: Child Behavior Questionnaire (CBQ)
detail.introduction: The Child Behavior Questionnaire (CBQ) is a caregiver-report measure designed to assess temperament in children. The CBQ assesses 15 or 16 dimensions of temperament, including Activity Level, Anger/Frustration, Fear, Inhibitory Control, Attentional Focusing, and Sadness. These are grouped into three main factors: Surgency/Extraversion, Negative Affect, and Effortful Control.

detail.title: Child Behaviour Checklist (CBCL/1½‑5)
detail.introduction: For the preschool version of the CBCL (CBCL/1½-5), parents or others who interact with the child in regular contexts rate the child's behavior. Respondents rate the child's behavior on a 3-point scale (not true, somewhat or sometimes true, and very true or often true), and are instructed to rate the behavior as it occurs now or within the previous two months. This delineation differs from the instructions on other age-versions, due to the fact that rapid development and behavioral changes in the preschool age range are common. The preschool checklist contains 100 problem behavior questions.

The sample was augmented with data from previous versions of the TRF of the statistical analysis, showing that there was no statistical difference in the groups. The sample included children who were not considered to have “serious behavioral/emotional problems” within the previous 12 months. The normative sample included the following demographic characteristics: 48% boys and 52% girls SES: 38% upper-class, 46% middle-class, 16% lower-class Ethnicity: 72% non-Latino White, 14% African American, 7% Latino, 7% Mixed or Other Region: 19% Northeast, 23% Midwest, 36% South, and 23% West

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: Participants from this study came from two Singapore samples of children between the ages of 6 and 12, a sample of referred children from CGC and a sample of non-referred children from the school/community. The sample comprised 71% boys and 29% girls. The reported ethnic classification of the children were as follows: 79% were Chinese, 10% were Malay, 7% were Indian, and 4% endorsed ‘‘Others’’. The CBCLs were completed by parents at the initial assessment at the clinic. Within the referred sample, 88% of the children received a diagnosis for a mental health disorder and subsequently received medical and/or psychosocial intervention. The main diagnoses given included Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorders (30%), Learning Disorders (18%), Conduct and Oppositional Defiant Disorders (7%), Pervasive Developmental/Autism Spectrum Disorders (6%), Anxiety Disorders (5%), and Adjustment and stress related disorders (6%). 447 children for the TRF.

listing.ages: 3 years old, 4 years old, 5 years old, 6 years old, 6+ years old

detail.title: Child Behaviour Questionnaire – Very Short Form (CBQ-VSF)
detail.introduction: The CBQ-VSF is a 36-item informant-report questionnaire assessing temperament of children (ages 3 – 8). The questionnaire is designed to capture three broad dimensions: surgency/extraversion, negative affectivity, and effortful control. Informants are asked to rate their child based on how they feel that their child’s reaction is likely to be in a variety of situations.

detail.title: Child Development Inventory (CDI)
detail.introduction: When a child’s development concerns parents or professionals, use the Child Development Inventory (CDI) to obtain the parent’s detailed report of the child’s present skills and possible problems and answer questions about a child’s school readiness. Parents complete the 300 item questionnaire at home or in your office and report their observations of the child’s behavior. It measures the child’s present development in eight areas: social, self-help, gross motor, fine motor, expressive language, language comprehension, letters, and numbers. It also includes a General Development Scale and 30 items to identify parent’s concerns about their child’s health and growth, vision and hearing, development and behavior

detail.title: Child Self-Regulation & Behaviour Questionnaire (CSBQ)
detail.introduction: The Child Self-Regulation & Behaviour Questionnaire (CSBQ) is a parent- or educator-report questionnaire consisting of 34 items pertaining to children’s everyday self-regulatory and social behaviours (e.g., ‘persists with difficult tasks’ and ‘waits their turn in activities’). For each item the respondent selects one of five options to indicate whether the statement is ‘Not true’ to ‘Very true’ about the child. The CSBQ produces measures of self-regulation (i.e., behavioural, cognitive and emotional), sociability, externalising, internalising and prosocial behaviour. iPad and paper versions are available.

detail.title: Classroom Assessment Scoring System (CLASS)
detail.introduction: The CLASS tool is a structured observation measure. It’s built on Teachstone’s Interaction Framework, which organizes the ways educators support children into three categories: to connect with them, to engage them, and to inspire their learning. To capture these interactions, the tool is organized into domains that reflect broad categories of educator–child interactions. Dimensions within each domain describe more specific aspects of those interactions.

fields.label: Proficiencies
fields.value: Social and emotional climate, Adult-child interactions, Cognitive stimulation, Physical environment, Peer interactions, Health and hygiene practices, Learning resources

fields.label: Prior qualifications/training required
fields.value: Observers must be Certified Class Observer. . This requires attending training, practicing with video, and passing an online certification test. Annual recertification is required.

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: Easy to Moderate. Dimension-level scores are calculated by totaling cycle scores and dividing by the number of cycles. Domain scores are the average of their corresponding dimension scores.

fields.label: Availability of guidance
fields.value: Comprehensive guidance available in updaed reference manual and the Observational Field Guide.

fields.label: Cost
fields.value: Reference manual is available for free download. Other components such as training and certification are fee-based.

detail.title: Cognitive Assessment System (CAS2)
detail.introduction: The Cognitive Assessment System, Second Edition (CAS2) is a well-researched, norm-referenced measure of cognitive ability based on the PASS theory of intelligence (Planning, Attention, Simultaneous, and Successive). The CAS2 measures cognitive processing abilities important for a broad range of differential diagnoses and instructional planning in individuals ages 5 through 18. The CAS2 provides practitioners with a valid and reliable tool to evaluate children’s strengths and weaknesses in important areas of cognitive processing.

detail.title: Cognitive Profiling System (CoPS)
detail.introduction: CoPS is a child-friendly assessment for ages 4-7 to identify cognitive strengths and challenges. Its nine short tests take 45-60 minutes in total to complete (and can be taken over a few sessions).The tests take the format of games that cover: working memory, phonological awareness, phonological processing, auditory discrimination and colour discrimination.Results are generated as graphical profiles which you can use with comprehensive ‘indications for actions’ tables and the teacher's manual to identify teaching strategies and interventions to suit the needs of each child.

detail.title: Comprehensive Assessment of Spoken Language-Second Edition (CASL®-2)
detail.introduction: The Comprehensive Assessment of Spoken Language-Second Edition is the most up-to-date measure of oral language skills available. It offers the flexibility of 14 stand-alone tests in one comprehensive yet specific battery. Preserving the strengths of the original and highly regarded test, the second edition introduces new and enhanced features to increase validity, functionality, and ease of use. Free scoring is available to all CASL-2 users through the WPS Online Evaluation System (OES).The CASL-2 shares the same underlying theory as the popular Oral and Written Language Scales-Second Edition (OWLS-II). Since both tests are based on the author's Integrative Language Theory, they provide a cohesive evaluation across a broad range of language areas. While the OWLS-II provides an evaluation of oral and written language, the CASL-2 offers a more in-depth picture of 14 spoken language skills.

detail.title: Comprehensive Executive Function Inventory (CEFI)
detail.introduction: The Comprehensive Executive Function Inventory™ (CEFI®) is a behavior rating scale of executive function strengths and weaknesses in youth 5 to 18 years. Executive function plays a crucial role in problem-solving and reasoning. When there are difficulties in this area, even the simplest tasks can become a significant challenge. Assessing a youth's executive function is vital for accurately diagnosing and developing an effective treatment plan.

detail.title: Concepts About Print
detail.introduction:
Concepts of Print is a criteria-referenced assessment which shows whether or not children in the pre-reading and early learning stages of reading understand:
- how a book works (e.g. front and back, pages)
- the conventions of print (e.g. left to right directionality and backward sweep)
- the important terminology needed for learning to read (e.g. picture, word, letter)

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The Concepts About Print (CAP) test was used in the Peep Learning Together Programme evaluation as a direct child assessment of early literacy skills. It was administered to nursery children aged 3 – 4 at both pre-test and post-test. In this trial, CAP served as the early literacy outcome measure and was also used analytically as a baseline covariate for language models, because the CELF language assessment was not administered at pre-test. This made CAP the only child-level literacy measure available before the intervention began.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the Peep Learning Together evaluation, the authors report baseline imbalance on CAP scores between intervention and control groups. The evaluation also notes that CAP was administered by nursery practitioners at baseline and by independent fieldworkers at follow-up, affecting comparability across time points.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: No structural adaptations were made to the CAP instrument. However, the evaluation implemented a procedural adaptation in which different assessors completed CAP at baseline and follow-up. Pre-test assessments were conducted by nursery practitioners, while post-test assessments were carried out by independent fieldworkers trained by the evaluation team. This change aimed to ensure both feasibility and consistency in post-test administration. In addition, CAP was used analytically as a proxy baseline literacy measure due to the absence of CELF pre-test data, though this constituted an analytic adjustment rather than a modification to the tool itself.

detail.title: Conceptual Interview on Scientific Understanding (CISU)
detail.introduction: The CISU is an individually administered, semi-structured interview designed to elicit students' talk about science concepts (specifically insects, metamorphosis, and pollination) and determine their expressive knowledge of target academic vocabulary. Children are shown five photographs (e.g., a ladybug eating aphids, a diagram of metamorphosis) and asked to describe what they see or explain how they would learn about a new insect.

detail.title: Conners Kiddie Continuous Performance test (Conners K‑CPT 2)
detail.introduction: The Conners Kiddie Continuous Performance Test 2 nd Edition™ (Conners K-CPT 2™) assesses attention deficits in children ages 4 to 7:11 years old. Based on the well-established Conners CPT paradigm, the Conners K–CPT 2 takes only half the time (7.5 minutes) to complete, making it more appropriate for younger children. Results from the measure can be used for clinical assessment, early identification, and educational classification. The assessment can also be used to evaluate treatment effectiveness by administering the test before treatment and during treatment to monitor change.

detail.title: Copy Design Task
detail.introduction: The Copy Design task instructs children to copy eight simple geometric designs. Children were allowed two attempts but no help from the assessor was allowed. The Copy Design task is a measure of persistence and sustained attention during a difficult task. This test has also been used previously to assess fine motor and visual control.

detail.title: Diagnostic Analysis of Nonverbal Accuracy, second edition (DANVA‑2)
detail.introduction: The DANVA-2 is a standardized assessment of a person’s ability to accurately decode non-verbal emotional cues (i.e., to recognise emotions from facial expressions, voices/tones (paralanguage), and in some versions body postures). It was designed to measure the ability to perceive the emotional states of others from their nonverbal behaviour.

listing.ages: 4 years old, 5 years old, 6 years old, 6+ years old

detail.title: Diagnostic Evaluation of Language Acquisition (DELV™ – NR)
detail.introduction: The DELV™ – Norm-Referenced is a norm-referenced diagnostic test designed to identify speech and language disorders/delays in children age 4.0-9.11 who speak all varieties of English. The DELV addresses four domains: Syntax, Pragmatics, Semantics, and Phonology. Both DELV assessments help educators limit assessment bias for speakers of non-Mainstream varieties of English.

detail.title: Dynamic Indicators of Basic Early Literacy Skills (DIBELS)
detail.introduction: DIBELS ® (Dynamic Indicators of Basic Early Literacy Skills) is a set of procedures and measures for assessing the acquisition of literacy skills. They are designed to be short (one minute) fluency measures that can be used to regularly detect risk and monitor the development of early literacy and early reading skills in kindergarten through eighth grade.The measures are consistent with many of the Common Core State Standards in Reading, especially those for Foundational Skills. When implemented as recommended, DIBELS results can be used to evaluate individual student development as well as provide grade-level feedback toward validated instructional objectives.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The ECERS‑E was used in the URLEY evaluation as one of the three observational rating scales assessing the quality of early years classroom provision. It extends ECERS‑3 by adding items focused on literacy, mathematics, science and environment, and diversity, offering a richer assessment of pedagogical practice. As with the other ERS tools, ECERS‑E was administered through a three-hour classroom observation, with items scored on a seven-point scale, where higher scores indicate higher quality. In URLEY, ECERS‑E (specifically its literacy subscale) was included both as a stand-alone outcome measure and as part of the composite ERS score used to evaluate the impact of the URLEY professional development programme on classroom quality. Observations were conducted in reception classrooms prior to randomisation and again in autumn 2017 by trained observers who were blind to trial assignment.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: No adaptations were made to the ECERS‑E instrument itself. All observations followed the standard scoring procedures, with trained A+ Education observers remaining blind to treatment allocation. The only notable adaptation was analytic: ECERS‑E contributed to a composite ERS outcome measure, combining items from ECERS‑3, ECERS‑E, and SSTEW. This did not alter the tool but shaped how it was used within the evaluation design.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: ECERS‑3 was used in the URLEY evaluation as one of the three Environment Rating Scales employed to assess the quality of early years classroom practice in nursery and reception settings. It was administered through a three-hour classroom observation, with observers scoring each item on a seven-point scale. ECERS‑3 captures multiple dimensions of classroom quality, including space and furnishings, personal care routines, language and literacy, learning activities, interactions, and programme structure. In URLEY, ECERS‑3 scores were collected before randomisation and again in autumn 2017, allowing the evaluation to measure change in quality over time in settings where teachers received URLEY training and mentoring. ECERS‑3 contributed to both the composite ERS score used as a secondary outcome and to separate analyses of overall classroom quality.

fields.label: Adaptations made

Observations were carried out by trained observers from A+ Education who remained blind to trial arm allocation to maintain objectivity. The only procedural adaptation was that ECERS‑3 was incorporated into a composite ERS outcome, combining selected items from ECERS‑3, ECERS‑E, and SSTEW for analysis. This analytic adaptation did not modify the instrument but determined how ECERS‑3 contributed to the evaluation outcomes.

detail.title: Early Childhood Inventory, 5th edition (ECI‑5)
detail.introduction: The Early Childhood Inventory-5 (ECI-5) is a behavior rating scale for DSM-5 emotional and behavioral disorders among preschool-aged children between 3 and 6 years old who are not yet attending elementary school (including kindergarten). There are both parent- and teacher-completed versions. The ECI-5: Parent Checklist contains 126 items for over two dozen emotional and behavioral disorders, and the ECI-5: Teacher Checklist contains 103 items. For each multi-item disorder there is an Impairment question (i.e., the degree to which symptoms interfere with the youth’s social or academic functioning).

detail.title: Early Communication Indicator (ECI)
detail.introduction:
The Early Communication Indicator (ECI) is one means of checking children’s growth toward the important outcome of being able to express themselves through their gestures, vocalizations, words, and sentences.
The Early Communication Indicator (ECI) for children birth to age 3 is a sensitive, easy to administer measure of communication (e.g., Luze et al., 2001). The ECI is a brief, repeatable, play-based, observational measure of a child’s communicative performance during a 6-minute play period with a familiar adult. The play session is standardized around one of two toys – either the Fisher-Price House or Fisher-Price Barn.

detail.title: Early Language Communication Instrument (ELCI)
detail.introduction: The ELCI is a rating scale that elicits information about a child’s observed receptive and expressive language and social/play skills. The ELCI can be completed by a Rater—a parent, caregiver, teacher, or daycare provider, then scored and interpreted by an Assessor—an SLP, school psychologist, neuropsychologist, or other professional. It can be used as a companion to directly administered tests and provides normative data in all three domains based on the reported observations, which can assist with eligibility and diagnostic information. The ELCI is especially helpful to use with children who are not able to participate in direct testing or who function differently across different environments.

detail.title: Early Movement Indicator (EMI)
detail.introduction: The Early Movement Indicator (EMI) is one means of checking children's growth toward the important general outcome of being able to move in a fluent and coordinated manner to play and participate in home, school, and community settings. The EMI is a play-based observational measure of a child's movement during a 6-minute play period with specific EMI toys and a familiar adult.

fields.value: Designed for early interventionists, early childhood educators, and researchers. Requires training/certification (available online).

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: Moderate. Requires coding behaviors either live or from video. “Data-driven decision making” is facilitated by online graphing tools.

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: Original Study (2002): Small sample of 29 infants and toddlers used to demonstrate feasibility. Updated Study (2018): Large sample of 628 children (contributing 2,258 assessments) from Early Head Start and Part C programs across five US states (Kansas, Missouri, Ohio, Texas, Washington). Infants/toddlers between 6 and 36 months of age at start participated. The mean age of children at the start of the project was 18 months, with a range of 6 to 36 months (SD = 9.5 months). The number of boys and girls was nearly evenly split at 50%. About 85% of children were from disadvantaged backgrounds based on the low-income eligibility requirements of EHS and included 15% of children with IFSPs. In total,35 (37%) of the 95 children with IFSPs had a movement concern identified. The majority home language reported was English (59%), followed by Spanish (36%) and other languages (5%).

fields.value: Greenwood, C.R., Walker, D., Buzhardt, J., Irvin, D., Schnitz, A.G. and Jia, F., 2018. Update on the EMI for infants and toddlers. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education, 38(2), pp.105-117.

detail.introduction: The Early Numeracy Test-Revised (ENT-r) is an activity-based assessment that evaluates a young child's early mathematical abilities, such as counting and prerequisite skills. fields.label: Floor effects
fields.value: In the ONE Programme evaluation, the authors report floor effects and administration or scoring issues affecting some EYT tasks, which limited score variation and required cautious handling of EYT data. In the School Starters study, the authors note that not all planned EYT subscales could be analysed due to non-normal score distributions and limited variance.

fields.label: Non-UK standardisation sample
fields.value: The toolbox was validated using a large sample of 1,764 children aged 2.5 to 5 years recruited from over 80 sites across four Australian states (NSW, VIC, SA, QLD). The sample was broadly representative of the Australian population in terms of sex with 946 males and 818 females (53.6% male, 46.4% female) and maternal education. It included an overrepresentation of Indigenous children (8.5%) and a slight bias toward lower SES areas.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The Early Years Toolbox has been used as a tablet-based assessment of early numeracy, language, and socio-emotional development in multiple EEF-funded studies. In the The ONE Programme trial, the EYT Numeracy task was used as the primary outcome measure to assess early mathematics attainment in 3 – 4‑year-old children, with testing conducted at baseline and endline. In the Concept Cat efficacy trial, the EYT Early Numeracy task is specified as a secondary outcome measure to assess early numeracy development alongside CELF-Preschool language measures. In the EEF School Starters COVID Impact Study, EYT subscales were used to measure Reception children’s numeracy, vocabulary, and socio-emotional development at the end of the school year.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the ONE Programme evaluation, the authors report floor effects and administration or scoring issues affecting some EYT tasks, which limited score variation and required cautious handling of EYT data. In the School Starters study, the authors note that not all planned EYT subscales could be analysed due to non-normal score distributions and limited variance.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: In the THE ONE trial, issues relating to scoring rule violations, baseline floor effects, and data coding errors affected analysis of some EYT outcomes, but no adaptations were made to the EYT instrument itself. In the School Starters COVID Impact Study, the planned longitudinal use of EYT was disrupted by COVID-19, with most assessments collected only at the end of the school year rather than across multiple timepoints. The study also noted that EYT was selected due to the lack of remotely administrable English-normed alternatives, which limited comparability with pre-pandemic norms.

fields.label: Source 1
fields.value: Howard, S.J. and Melhuish, E., 2017. An early years toolbox for assessing early executive function, language, self-regulation, and social development: Validity, reliability, and preliminary norms. Journal of psychoeducational assessment, 35(3), pp.255-275.

The toolbox was validated using a large sample of 1,764 children aged 2.5 to 5 years recruited from over 80 sites across four Australian states (NSW, VIC, SA, QLD). The sample was broadly representative of the Australian population in terms of sex with 946 males and 818 females (53.6% male, 46.4% female) and maternal education. It included an overrepresentation of Indigenous children (8.5%) and a slight bias toward lower SES areas.

Insight from EEF Early Years Trials
Description of use(s)
The Early Years Toolbox has been used as a tablet-based assessment of early numeracy, language, and socio-emotional development in multiple EEF-funded studies. In the The ONE Programme trial, the EYT Numeracy task was used as the primary outcome measure to assess early mathematics attainment in 3 – 4‑year-old children, with testing conducted at baseline and endline. In the Concept Cat efficacy trial, the EYT Early Numeracy task is specified as a secondary outcome measure to assess early numeracy development alongside CELF-Preschool language measures. In the EEF School Starters COVID Impact Study, EYT subscales were used to measure Reception children’s numeracy, vocabulary, and socio-emotional development at the end of the school year.

Key Learnings
In the ONE Programme evaluation, the authors report floor effects and administration or scoring issues affecting some EYT tasks, which limited score variation and required cautious handling of EYT data. In the School Starters study, the authors note that not all planned EYT subscales could be analysed due to non-normal score distributions and limited variance.

Adaptations made
In the THE ONE trial, issues relating to scoring rule violations, baseline floor effects, and data coding errors affected analysis of some EYT outcomes, but no adaptations were made to the EYT instrument itself. In the School Starters COVID Impact Study, the planned longitudinal use of EYT was disrupted by COVID-19, with most assessments collected only at the end of the school year rather than across multiple timepoints. The study also noted that EYT was selected due to the lack of remotely administrable English-normed alternatives, which limited comparability with pre-pandemic norms.

detail.title: ELOM Home Learning Environment Questionnaire
detail.introduction:
A child’s early learning and development is influenced at the home – their first early learning environment. The ELOM Home Learning Environment (HLE) Tool is a short questionnaire designed to measure home aspects associated with early language, numeracy and cognitive functioning for children aged 2-7 years old.During a 15-minute interview the primary caregiver is asked questions about themselves and their child(ren). The ELOM HLE assesses the following:The Early Learning Resources Score: the total number of children’s books in the home and the availability of bought or homemade toys, household utensils and other objects used for play.
The Early Learning Activities Score: early learning activities conducted with the child at home, including reading, telling stories, singing songs, going out together, playing, naming things, counting, drawing and painting.
Caregiver Time with the Child Score: the amount of time a caregiver has spent with the child in the week and during the weekend.

detail.title: Emotion regulation Checklist (ERC)
detail.introduction: The Emotion Regulation Checklist (ERC) is a 24-item measure of children’s self-regulation. The ERC can be answered by adults well acquainted with the child, such as the father, mother, caregiver, or teacher. It was designed to assess the child’s ability to manage and to cope with emotions.. The ERC items assess affective stability, intensity, valence, flexibility, and situational appropriateness of children between the ages of 3 to 12 years, but it has also been applied to younger children.

detail.title: Emotional and Behavioral Screener (EBS)
detail.introduction: The Emotional and Behavioral Screener (EBS) is an accurate and efficient instrument that uses teachers’ ratings to identify students in grades K-12 who show signs of potential emotional or behavioral problems and who warrant careful observation, further assessment, or provision of more than the usual educational service.

fields.label: Prior qualifications/training required
fields.value: None specified. It is designed to be used by researchers, educational professionals, school district administrators, or principals.

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: Easy. The EBS Rating Form contains 10 items, each of which describes a specific and observable problem. This form is used to record the student’s identifying information; to note each EBS item; to document EBS scores; and to make comments, interpretations, or recommendations. The EBS Decision Summary Form provides a convenient way to record and keep track of multiple scores; to summarize the EBS results; and to indicate directions for further assessment and intervention

fields.label: Cost
fields.value: Rating form and Decision summary forms available for $38.50 each (for a pack of 50)

fields.label: Non-UK standardisation sample
fields.value: The study sample consisted of 2,234 students drawn from the EBS norming sample. Of these, 1,138 students had a verified emotional disturbance (ED) and 1,096 students had no identified disability. Ages ranged from 5 to 17 years (mean age = 11.34, SD = 3.42). Elementary students (ages 5 – 11) comprised 1,128 participants, and secondary students (ages 12 – 17) comprised 1,106 participants. The sample was 65.9% male (n = 1,472) and racially diverse (63.6% White, 21.8% African American, 6.6% Hispanic, <1% Asian, <1% Native American, 6.3% other). The authors state that the norming sample closely matched U.S. census distributions for age, gender, race/ethnicity, and socioeconomic status.

detail.title: Emotional Availability scales
detail.introduction: The Emotional Availability Scales (EA Scales) measures the quality of parent-child or adult-child interactions. Emotional availability refers to 'the adult's 'receptive presence' to the child's emotional signals'". The scales capture "a dyad's emotional connection in observational settings by four parental and two child-related scales

fields.value: Raters completed a three-day online training as a requirement for application. Reliability certification is required.

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: Easy. Item scores within a dimension are summed to create a composite dimension score. The sum score for each of the six dimensions ranges from seven to 29.

fields.label: Availability of guidance
fields.value: Manual and various forms of training available from publisher.

fields.label: Time required
fields.value: Rating is performed on ten minutes of video material or longer interactions of 15 – 20 minutes.

fields.value: Not stated for the test. The fee-based training for raters costs $603 per person and is valid for two years.

fields.value: The tool has been applied to various clinical and non-clinical population. One Australian sample was of 157, while another German sample was of 116 parent-child dyads. Another study was conducted for sixty-two Dutch parent-child dyads. Recruitment for the various studies as usually conducted in hospitals/clinics. No explicit mention of stratification or norming in the available studies

detail.title: First Year inventory (FYI)
detail.introduction: The First-Year Inventory (Baranek, Watson, Crais & Reznick, 2003; FYI) is a parent-report questionnaire developed by our team as a general population-screening tool to identify 12-month-old infants who might be at-risk for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) or a related developmental disorder. The FYI covers two broad developmental domains: social communication and sensory regulatory functions. The two domains are further defined by eight specific constructs: social orienting and receptive communication, social-affective engagement, imitation, expressive communication, sensory processing, regulatory patterns, reactivity, and repetitive behavior.

detail.title: Grammar and Phonology Screening test (GAPS)
detail.introduction:
The ‘Grammar and Phonology Screening’ (GAPS) Test is a standardised, quick
screening tool for language impairment. It is a short, reliable assessment of young
children’s language abilities. It is individually administered and designed to assess
whether pre-school and early school entry children have the necessary grammar and
pre-reading phonological skills needed for education and social development.

detail.title: Grass – Snow Task
detail.introduction: A measure used to assess young children's ability to inhibit a prepotent response, a component of executive function, by performing the opposite action to a simple rule. In the task, a child is shown two cards (typically green and white) and must learn to touch the green card when the experimenter says "snow" and the white card when they say "grass"

detail.title: Head-Toes-Knees-Shoulders
detail.introduction: HTKS is a direct assessment tool used to measure self-regulation in young children. It involves asking children to perform physical actions that contradict verbal instructions, testing their ability to inhibit a natural response and follow a new rule.

fields.value: Easy.Each item is scored as: 0 (Incorrect) 1 (Self-correct: initial motion to incorrect, but ends with correct) 2 (Correct) Total Score: Scores range from 0 to 60 (30 items total).

fields.label: Non-UK standardisation sample
fields.value: 1,386 children across three samples from Michigan and Oregon. The first sample was collected in predominantly middle- to upper-SES suburban area with a range of ethnic diversity in southeast Michigan. Participants included 351 (51% female) children followed from preschool through second grade. The second sample consisted of 642 (51% female) preschool aged children from middle-SES communities with data waves collected over four years in Michigan as part of the Michigan Longitudinal Study of Early Literacy Development. The third sample was recruited from a mixed-SES rural site in Oregon and consisted of 393 (50% female) children followed from preschool through kindergarten as part of a measurement study focused on improving measures of school readiness and selfregulation.

detail.title: Head-Toes-Knees-Shoulders – Revised
detail.introduction: The Head-Toes-Knees-Shoulders Revised (HTKS-R) is a revised version of the Head-Toes-Knees-Shoulders (HTKS) task, used to assess self-regulation in young children. It involves asking children to perform physical actions that contradict verbal instructions, testing their ability to inhibit a natural response and follow a new rule. The HTKS-R includes a downward extension to better capture variability in children with lower self-regulation skills.

fields.label: Floor effects
fields.value: In the ONE Programme evaluation, the authors report that HTKS‑R was more complex for assessors to administer than other measures in the battery. The evaluation documents substantial floor effects, particularly at baseline, with many children unable to progress beyond early items. The authors also report recording and scoring errors, linked to difficulties applying stopping rules consistently, which reduced the usable HTKS‑R data at baseline despite assessor training.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: In the ONE Programme efficacy trial, HTKS‑R was used as a secondary outcome measure of executive functioning. It was administered one-to-one by trained, blinded assessors to children aged 3 – 4 years at both baseline and endline, as part of a fixed assessment battery that also included the Early Years Toolbox Numeracy and Corsi Blocks tasks. Administration followed the standard HTKS‑R protocol, including prescribed stopping rules and scoring procedures.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the ONE Programme evaluation, the authors report that HTKS‑R was more complex for assessors to administer than other measures in the battery. The evaluation documents substantial floor effects, particularly at baseline, with many children unable to progress beyond early items. The authors also report recording and scoring errors, linked to difficulties applying stopping rules consistently, which reduced the usable HTKS‑R data at baseline despite assessor training.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: The authors report that additional assessor training and clarification of scoring procedures were introduced between baseline and endline in response to administration and recording difficulties. While these adjustments reduced the frequency of administration errors at endline, floor effects persisted for a proportion of the sample. No structural changes were made to the HTKS‑R instrument itself.

fields.value: Gonzales, C. R., Bowles, R., Geldhof, G. J., Cameron, C. E., Tracy, A., & McClelland, M. M. (2021). The Head-Toes-Knees-Shoulders Revised (HTKS-R): Development and psychometric properties of a revision to reduce floor effects. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 56, 320-332.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The Home Learning Environment (HLE) Index was used across several EEF evaluations as a parent-reported measure of the frequency and quality of learning activities in the home, such as shared reading, language-rich interactions, and engagement with early literacy and numeracy. In the PACT evaluation, the HLE Index was administered to parents of Reception-aged children (4 – 5 years) at immediate post-test and again five months later. In the ParentChild+ evaluation, it was used with parents of children aged 2 – 3 years as a secondary outcome measure. In the Peep Learning Together Programme, the HLE Index was administered to parents of nursery-aged children (3 – 4 years) to capture changes in home learning practices associated with programme participation. In the School Starters study, the HLE Index was included in parent surveys completed by families of Reception children (4 – 5 years) across multiple time points during the academic year.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the ParentChild+ and Peep Learning Together evaluations, the authors report reliance on parent self-report for HLE data. Across these evaluations, the authors note high levels of missing data at follow-up, which affected the completeness of HLE datasets.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: No adaptations were made to the HLE Index itself in any of the trials. However, administrative adjustments occurred across studies. In PACT, the HLE Index was administered at two different follow-up points to capture both immediate and sustained effects, though data loss at post-test limited interpretability. In ParentChild+, the measure was administered online or in person depending on COVID-19 restrictions, and parent self-report was used as the primary mode of data collection. In the COVID School Starters study, the HLE Index was embedded within broader parent surveys distributed during periods of remote schooling. In Peep, the measure was integrated into existing parent questionnaires completed in the nursery setting. These procedural variations did not alter the structure or scoring of the HLE Index.

detail.title: Home Observation for measurement of the Environment (HOME-21)
detail.introduction: The HOME-SF is a modification of the HOME inventory (Caldwell and Bradley 1984, 1992), a unique observational measure of the quality of the cognitive stimulation and emotional support provided by a child's family. The HOME-SF is about half as long as the original HOME Inventory, an adaptation necessitated by survey time and cost constraints. More than half of the HOME-SF's items are multi-response maternal reports that were reworded, with the assistance of the instrument's designers, from the original HOME Inventory's dichotomous observer ratings.In addition to the overall HOME-SF score, the Child file includes two subscores: a cognitive stimulation and emotional support score. These are also described below.

fields.label: Proficiencies
fields.value: Physical environment, Social and emotional climate, Adult-child interactions, Health and hygiene routines, Learning resources, Cognitive stimulation, Peer interactions

fields.label: Respondent
fields.value: Mother for Mother Supplement and for remaining, observer

fields.label: Prior qualifications/training required
fields.value: The HOME-21 is designed for use by researchers, practitioners, and community professionals and does not require specialist clinical qualifications according to this article.

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: Scoring is straightforward and involves dichotomising item responses using predefined cut-offs and computing the mean across items. The authors explicitly describe the tool as suitable for implementation in applied community and clinical settings.

fields.label: Availability of guidance
fields.value: Scoring rules and original item derivations are available through the HOME-SF documentation and the National Longitudinal Survey codebooks referenced by the authors.

fields.label: Floor effects
fields.value: In the EasyPeasy evaluation, the authors report that HOME was administered through researcher-led home visits combining observation and parent interview. The evaluation notes that the resource-intensive nature of HOME limited its administration to a small subsample of families.

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: Two independent U.S. samples were used. The Fast Track sample included 553 parents of children aged 0 – 17 years. The Great Smoky Mountains Study sample included 722 parents of children aged 0 – 17 years. The combined sample size was 1,275 participants.The Fast Track sample included 49.2% female parents and was 48.1% Black and 51.9% White/other, drawn from four U.S. regions. The Great Smoky Mountains Study sample included 54.7% female parents and was 67.6% White, 6.6% Black, and 25.8% American Indian, drawn from 11 counties in western North Carolina. Both samples were community-based longitudinal cohorts with socioeconomic diversity.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The HOME measure was used in the EasyPeasy: Learning Through Play trial as a secondary outcome measure to assess changes in the home learning environment of children aged 3 – 4 years. It was administered through a researcher home visit, which included a parent interview and direct observation of the home environment while the child was present. The Early Childhood HOME version was used, consisting of 55 binary-scored items grouped into six learning-relevant subscales: learning materials, language stimulation, responsivity, academic stimulation, modelling, and variety of activities and parental interaction. The HOME was administered to a self-selected subsample of 50 households, split evenly between intervention and control groups, at both pre- and post-intervention.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the EasyPeasy evaluation, the authors report that HOME was administered through researcher-led home visits combining observation and parent interview. The evaluation notes that the resource-intensive nature of HOME limited its administration to a small subsample of families.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: No structural adaptations were made to the HOME instrument itself. However, the study design restricted HOME administration to a small volunteer subsample, rather than the full trial cohort, due to feasibility constraints. HOME analysis was also conducted without adjustment for baseline HOME scores, as the measure was collected post-randomisation. These represent methodological adaptations to implementation and analysis, rather than changes to the HOME tool itself.

detail.title: Individualized Student Instruction (ISI) Coding System
detail.introduction: The ISI system codes duration of time each child is experiencing a given type of instructional activity (e.g., literacy, math etc.) or noninstructional activity (e.g., transitioning, waiting for the teacher to give directions, listening to directions/planning, going off-task etc.). The ISI system also records duration of time children are in a given context (e.g., whole-class, individual, or peer) and who is managing the child’s attention (e.g., the child, peers, or the teacher).

detail.title: Infant Behavior Report questionnaire – Revised
detail.introduction: The original IBQ was developed by Dr. Rothbart in the early 1980s and first reported in the 1981 Child Development article, “Measurement of Temperament in Infancy” (Rothbart, 1981).This early form of the instrument assessed 6 domains of infant temperament (activity level, soothability, fear, distress to limitations, smiling and laughter, and duration of orienting). Dr. Rothbart and her colleague, Dr. Masha Gartstein, revised the IBQ by refining the original scales and adding several new scales. The new instrument is referred to as the IBQ-Revised (IBQ-R).

detail.title: Infant Language Link
detail.introduction: Infant Language Link is an innovative, award-winning online assessment and intervention package used by schools to identify and support pupils, aged 4-8 years, with language and communication needs. It is also suitable for learners new to English.

fields.label: Floor effects
fields.value: In the Infant Language Link evaluation, the authors report that the standardised screening tool was valued by school staff for identifying pupils with language needs and for providing more specific information about individual children’s language profiles. The report notes that screening data increased staff confidence in identifying need, but also highlights that the volume of identified needs placed additional demands on school resources, shaping how screening information could be acted upon in practice.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: In the EEF Infant Language Link efficacy trial, Infant Language Link was used as a whole-school programme combining a standardised language screening tool with tiered classroom and targeted support. For the purposes of the evaluation, it was delivered to Year 1 pupils aged 5 – 6, with all pupils in the participating class screened at the start of the school year using the Infant Language Link screening assessment. Screening results were used to identify pupils for targeted small-group intervention, while all pupils received whole-class strategies implemented by teachers. Outcome assessments were administered by independent, blinded speech and language therapists at baseline and post-test using standardised language measures selected in agreement with the developer.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the Infant Language Link evaluation, the authors report that the standardised screening tool was valued by school staff for identifying pupils with language needs and for providing more specific information about individual children’s language profiles. The report notes that screening data increased staff confidence in identifying need, but also highlights that the volume of identified needs placed additional demands on school resources, shaping how screening information could be acted upon in practice.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: The authors report several adaptations to usual programme delivery for the purposes of the evaluation. Unlike standard practice, where Infant Language Link typically begins in Reception and continues through Year 1 and Year 2, the trial focused solely on Year 1 pupils, meaning all children received their first exposure to the programme in that year. In addition, the timeframe for delivering targeted sessions was compressed, with schools instructed to deliver two targeted sessions per week rather than the usual weekly session, and to implement a fixed sequence of intervention groups rather than tailoring group selection based on screening results. These adaptations were made to fit the evaluation timeframe and ensure consistency across schools.

fields.value: Enlow, M.B., White, M.T., Hails, K., Cabrera, I. and Wright, R.J., 2016. The Infant Behavior Questionnaire-Revised: Factor structure in a culturally and sociodemographically diverse sample in the United States. Infant Behavior and Development, 43, pp.24-35.

detail.title: Infant-Toddler Developmental Assessment-Second Edition (IDA‑2)
detail.introduction: The Infant-Toddler Developmental Assessment-Second Edition (IDA-2) is a comprehensive, multidisciplinary, family-centered six-phase process designed to identify children birth to 3 years of age who are developmentally at risk. The IDA-2 includes the Provence Birth-to-Three Developmental Profile, a criterion-referenced measure of development in eight areas: (1) gross motor, (2) fine motor, (3) relationship to inanimate objects, (4) language/communication, (5) self-help, (6) relationship to persons, (7) emotions and feeling states, and (8) coping behavior.

detail.title: Infant Toddler Social Emotional assessment (ITSEA)
detail.introduction: The Brief Infant-Toddler Social and Emotional Assessment (BITSEA) is an instrument that can be used to briefly screen children’s social or emotional behavior problems and competencies. This brief instrument is based on the Infant Toddler Social Emotional Assessment (ITSEA); both the BITSEA and ITSEA were designed to identify deficits or delays in these domains. Authors advise administering the ITSEA in follow-up for children with positive scores on the BITSEA.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: LanguageScreen was used as a tablet-based standardised assessment of oral language in large-scale EEF-funded evaluations. In the NELI Wave 2 national scale-up, LanguageScreen was used as the primary outcome measure to assess receptive and expressive language, listening comprehension, and sentence repetition in Reception-aged children (4 – 5 years). It was also used at baseline as a screening tool to identify the pupils with the weakest language skills for programme eligibility. In the PACT trial, LanguageScreen was used as the delayed post-test primary language outcome measure after COVID-19 prevented immediate post-intervention testing. Children were assessed at the end of Reception, approximately ten months after intervention delivery, with LanguageScreen replacing the originally planned battery of face-to-face standardised language tests.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the School Starters evaluation, the authors report that LanguageScreen was used both as a screening tool at baseline and as an outcome measure at follow-up. The evaluation notes variability in administration mode and timing, including delivery by school staff rather than independent assessors and delayed post-testing, which shaped how LanguageScreen data were collected and analysed.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: In the NELI Wave 2 scale-up, LanguageScreen served both as a screening tool and outcome measure, but no structural adaptations to the assessment itself were reported. However, schools were not required to use LanguageScreen for pupil selection and could rely on professional judgement instead. In the PACT trial, major procedural adaptations occurred due to COVID-19. The originally planned in-person standardised language assessments at immediate post-test were cancelled, and LanguageScreen was introduced as a replacement delayed post-test outcome measure. Additionally, LanguageScreen assessments were delivered by school staff rather than blinded researchers, which represented a substantial change to the original evaluation design rather than to the instrument itself.

detail.title: LENA’s Developmental Snapshot (LDS)
detail.introduction: This 52-item survey was designed to assess expressive and receptive language skills in children 2 months to 36 months and to estimate developmentalage as a function of chronological age.

fields.label: Publisher/author name
fields.value: J. Richards, C. R. Greenwood and J. K Montgomery

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: Easy. Automated scoring. Generates a language evelopment age and age-referenced standard score to facilitate flexible interpretation.

fields.label: Availability of guidance
fields.value: Yes. Explanations and examples for potentially ambiguous items were included as needed in the snapshot to help parents complete the Snapshot without professional guidance.

fields.label: Non-UK standardisation sample
fields.value: 308 families (Scoring Sample), subset of 59 families (Monthly Sample) for longitudinal data. Recruitment for this original study involved sending 6,000 recruitment postcards to parents in the Denver-metro area. Interested parents completed a phone interview providing information on household demographics and child language skills. Selected families (n = 329) were from monolingual English-speaking households, reported no language or other developmental delays, and were targeted on the US census on mother’s attained education as a proxy for socioeconomic status. Eighty percent (248) were no older than 36 months, and 92% were 42 months or younger. Data for older children were incorporated into the initial scoring algorithm, but for valuation analyses, the typically developing sample was restricted to ages 36 months or younger.

detail.title: List Sort Working Memory Test
detail.introduction:
The List Sorting Working Memory test is an assessment of working memory. Participants ages 5 and older are asked to recall and sequence different stimuli that are presented visually and via audio. Pictures of different foods and animals are displayed on the screen with written text and
an accompanying audio recording that names the picture/item. The participant is asked to say
the names of the items back to the examiner in size order from smallest to largest.

detail.title: MacArthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories
detail.introduction: This is a standardised parents reporting system. The infant version looks at comprehension, word production and symbolic and communicative gesture. The toddler version explores word production and the early stages of grammar. It is a ‘by-parent report’, takes 20–40 minutes to complete and 10–15 minutes to score and has norms up to 37 months. Though it was developed in the USA and Canada, it’s used in many research studies and can be useful in the UK.

Although these 2007 expanded norms more closely approximate national demographic statistics than the original 2,000 norms, the developers note that the sample still underrepresents children and families with low educational and/or socioeconomic backgrounds. detail.title: MacArthur Health and Behaviour Questionnaire (HBQ)
detail.introduction: The original HBQ (version 1.0) was designed to collect data from adult reporters about children between the ages of 4 and 8 years. The HBQ comprises multiple scales that measure children’s mental health symptoms (e.g., Internalizing and Externalizing Symptoms and their subscales), physical health (e.g., Chronic Medical Conditions, Global Physical Health), social functioning (e.g., Peer Acceptance and Rejection, Prosocial Behaviors), and school functioning (e.g., Academic Competence, School Engagement). The HBQ also includes measures of children’s health care utilization in the mental, physical, and school domains. Versions of the instrument have been created for both parent (HBQ-P 1.0) and teacher (HBQ-T 1.0) report.

detail.title: MacArthur Story Stem battery
detail.introduction: This tool is the MacArthur Story Stem Battery, a systematic collection of story beginnings that are referred to as 'stems'. These stems are designed to elicit information from children about their representational worlds. This method is particularly exciting because using it allows developmental psychologists to gain information directly from children about their emotional states and what they are able to understand, and in turn, to use this information to explore significant emotional differences among children.

detail.title: Manual Measuring Early Learning Environment (MELE)
detail.introduction: The design of MELE was led by the World Bank, UNICEF, UNESCO, and the Brookings Institution. The MELE includes a classroom observation tool, a teacher and director survey, and a parent survey. Quality is measured through six constructs: Environments and materials, teacher-child interactions, Pedagogy and Approaches to learning, Family and Community Engagement, Inclusion, and Play

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: A sample of 250 schools (85% private, which reflected the pro portion of private to public schools across the country) across four country zones (defined by regional ecology and represent ing all regions of the country) were recruited for participation in the MELQO study based on government lists. Some private prepri mary facilities were not included in government lists because they were not known or registered with the government, so sampling should not be considered comprehensive. Children were nested in classrooms (one classroom per school), with one main teacher serving as the focal point of the observation and providing infor mation on children’s social/emotional development. From each classroom, approximately 4 children were randomly selected to complete measures of child development and learning for a total sample size of 979 children (46% male; mean age = 5.49 years [SD = 0.54]). Classroom observations, which were used to complete the MELE‑A, lasted on average 2.02 h (SD = 0.71) and took place in the morning during a scheduled visit. On average, teachers reported 9.10 years of preprimary experience (SD = 7.31) and nearly half (49%) received professional development in the past 12 months. The average classroom had 19.94 children (ranging from 2 to 200; SD =17.12).

detail.title: MARKO‑D test
detail.introduction: With MARKO-D, a child-friendly individual test is available that can be used to examine the prerequisites for later school development with regard to acquired arithmetic concepts. The test consists of 55 items that assess the following five concepts (which represent successive developmental levels): counting number, ordinal number line, cardinality and decomposability, inclusion and class inclusion, as well as relationality.
