detail.title: Maternal Behavior Q‑Sort (MBQS; regular and short version)
detail.introduction: The MBQS is typically used to measure the sensitivity of mothers of infants aged 8 months up to 3.5 years. A standard version of the MBQS requires an observer to assess the behaviour of the mother based on 90 different descriptions. The 90 items assess the mother's accessibility, responsiveness and promptness to the child's needs. The score is generated by observing the interaction between the mother and child in the home, playground or laboratory, and is usually filmed. It can take anywhere between 40 minutes and 2 hours to complete, in addition to the time required for coding.

detail.title: Measuring Early Learning and Quality Outcomes (MELQO)
detail.introduction:
MELQO used existing measures and the expertise of a technical advisory group to create two measurement modules, one aimed at measuring child
development and early learning (MODEL) and one focused on measuring the quality of early learning environments (MELE) in pre-school and the early grades (beginning with
classroom-based settings).MODEL – which stands for Measure of Development and Early Learning - measures children’s learning and development through two tools, a direct assessment and a teacher/
caregiver survey, designed to assess the basic domains of children’s development at the start of school, including executive function, social–emotional development and pre-academic skills (early mathematics and literacy skills).MELE – which stands for Measure of Early Learning Environments – includes seven domains for quality in early learning environments: play, pedagogy, interactions, environment,
parent/community engagement,
personnel and inclusion.

detail.title: Measuring Early Learning Quality and Outcomes (MELQO)
detail.introduction: The Measuring Early Learning Quality and Outcomes (MELQO) initiative began in 2014 in anticipation of this new global emphasis on early childhood development (ECD). Led by UNESCO, the World Bank, the Center for Universal Education at the Brookings Institution and UNICEF, the initiative aims to promote feasible, accurate and useful measurement of children’s development and learning at the start of primary school, and of the quality of their pre-primary learning environments. Items are designed for children between the ages of 4 and 6 years

detail.title: Memory Validity Profile (MVP)
detail.introduction: The MVP is the first performance validity test (PVT) specifically designed for and nationally standardized on children, adolescents, and young adults. It is conormed with the Child and Adolescent Memory Profile (ChAMP), which provides comprehensive information about learning and memory and an embedded indicator of validity. Age-adjusted cutoff scores minimize false positives in younger children, and because there are no motor requirements, it can be administered to individuals with varying abilities.

fields.label: Non-UK standardisation sample
fields.value: The final standardization sample consists of 1221 individuals from 15 age groups, combining 18 and 19 year old into one group, 20 and 21 years into one group, and then including age groups of each year from 5 through 17 years. Each age group consists of 79 to 85 individuals for age groups from 5 to 17, with 69 individuals in the 18 – 19 group and 66 in the 20 – 21 group. detail.title: Narrative Competence task (NCT)
detail.introduction: The NCT is a storytelling task developed to assess narrative competence in Italian children aged 3–8 years. The NCT is an 18-picture storybook created to elicit children’s narratives. The story is about two children, a boy and a girl who meet in a park and play with a ball together. Unintentionally, they throw the ball into a tree and then have to try to get it back in different ways. At the end of the story, a policeman helps the children to get the ball back, and they resume playing. The NCT was developed with respect to typical story grammar (presentation of the characters, problematic situation, attempts to solve the problem, solution, and conclusion of the story). The situation that is described is familiar to children because the events that are included represent what can occasionally occur in a park, and the images are sufficiently simple to be immediately clear.

fields.label: Proficiencies
fields.value: Expressive vocabulary, Narrative skills, Narrative, Receptive vocabulary, Syntax, Morphology, Grammar, Inferencing, Language reasoning

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: Complex. The NCT is scored by transcribing the recording of children’s narrative retellings and analysing them. The NCT is scored by counting how much story content and linguistic complexity a child produces. Coders total the number of key events and agents mentioned, check whether the child includes each of the eight key story passages, tally the number of different mental state words used and calculate lexical diversity (D index) and mean length of utterance

fields.value: Available for research purposes only / non-commercial

The participants were randomly selected among the children attending the schools.

detail.title: New Reynell Developmental Language Scales (NRDLS)
detail.introduction:
Identify speech and language delays and impairments from an early age.
A widely used and reliable assessment for gaining a diagnostic overview of the language ability of children aged from 2 years to 7 years 6 months, NRDLS assesses both production and understanding of language, to help you guide intervention and evaluate its effectiveness.NRDLS is made up of two closely aligned scales: the Comprehension Scale explores aspects of a child’s understanding of selected vocabulary items and grammatical features, and the Production Scale examines a child’s production of the same features of language.Assessments are carried out using a mix of play-based activities that capture children’s attention, with three appealing characters that they can handle and direct to support their completion of the tasks.

detail.title: Number Knowledge Test
detail.introduction: The Number Knowledge Test was devised to measure the conceptual knowledge of number (number sense) that the average child has available at the age levels of 4, 6, 8, and 10 years. This knowledge has been referred to elsewhere as a set of “central conceptual structures for number” and “powerful organizing schemas” that help children make sense of quantitative problems. Research has shown that the knowledge assessed at each age level of this test is essential for successfully learning arithmetic in school and foundational for higher mathematics learning

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: The clinical validation sample comprised 3,070 caregivers reporting on children and youth aged 4 – 17 years, and 1,959 youth aged 12 – 17 years providing self-reports. Test – retest reliability was evaluated in a separate subsample of 99 caregiver – youth dyads assessed twice over a 7 – 14-day interval. Participants were drawn from a large tertiary outpatient mental health service in Ontario, Canada. Caregivers reported on 908 children aged 4 – 11 years (mean age = 8.7 years, SD = 2.0) and 2,162 youth aged 12 – 17 years (mean age = 14.7 years, SD = 1.5). Youth self-reports included 1,959 adolescents aged 12 – 17 years. The caregiver sample was 58.8 % male for children and 27.9 % male for youth. The majority of children were born in Canada (94 – 96 %). Sampling was clinical and site-based rather than population-random.

detail.title: Ortiz Picture Vocabulary Acquisition Test (Ortiz PVAT)
detail.introduction: The Ortiz PVAT is a receptive vocabulary assessment that can be used to assess both English speakers and English learners. With unique dual norms (English speaker norms as well as English learner norms that control for exposure to English), the Ortiz PVAT makes it possible to evaluate an individual from any language background, determine whether an individual’s English vocabulary performance follows expected patterns (as either a native English speaker or an English learner), or rather, is suggestive of a language problem or disorder.

detail.title: Parent-Child Early Relational Assessment (ERA)
detail.introduction: The Parent-Child Early Relational Assessment (ERA) (Clark, 1985, 2006, 2010, 2015) was designed to measure the quality of affect and behavior in parent-child interactions. The instrument uses ratings that are based on observations of 5-minute videotaped interactions during feeding, structured task, or free play. The purpose of the ERA is to attempt to capture the child’s experience of the parent, the parents’ experience of the child, the affective and behavioral characteristics that each bring to the interaction, and the quality or tone of the relationship.

detail.title: Penn Interactive Peer Play Scale (PIPPS)
detail.introduction: The Penn Interactive Peer Play Scale (PIPPS) is a behavioral rating instrument useful for understanding peer play behaviors and for meeting the need for congruent play assessment measures for parents and teachers across settings during early childhood. This assessment system consists of parallel versions of parent and teacher rating scales, as well as parallel versions for use in preschool and kindergarten. The parent version assesses play in the home and neighborhood, whereas the teacher version examines play in the classroom and at school. Each version consists of 32 four-point Likert-scale items, which indicate how often the parent or teacher has observed the behavior during free play in the previous two months (i.e., “never,” “seldom,” “often,” or “always”). The items assess both competencies and needs within play to identify children who demonstrate successful peer relationships and those who have difficulties with peers.

detail.title: Phonological Assessment Battery (PhAB2 Primary)
detail.introduction: A toolkit to identify pupils with phonological difficulties. Accurately identify children who have phonological difficulties and need additional help to process and use the sounds in spoken language.The Phonological Assessment Battery 2 (PhAB2) Primary, provides revised versions of the six standardised tests in the original assessment, as well as four new tests, in line with the latest research in phonological awareness. Targeted testing ranges for 5–6 and 7–11-year-olds provide more sensitive assessments to give you a greater understanding of a child’s phonological strengths and weaknesses.

detail.title: Pictorial scale of Physical Self-Concept for younger Children (P‑PSC‑C)
detail.introduction: The Pictorial Scale of Perceived Physical Self-Concept for Young Children (P-PSC-C) is a version of the Physical Self-Description Questionnaire for Children (PSC-C; Dreiskämper et al., 2015) extended by illustrations for an age-based measuring of elementary school children’s physical self-concept. The PSC-C is in turn based on the Physical Self-Description Questionnaire (PSDQ; Marsh et al., 1994), which was developed for assessing adolescents’ and adults’ physical self-concept, and adapted on the elementary school-age. There is a total of seven subscales (endurance, flexibility, strength, coordination, velocity, sport competence, appearance), each consisting of three items. The item verbalizations were taken over from the PSC-C, extended by illustrations, and can be answered on a 4-point-scale: For each item, the children are shown a figure achieving a high score on the item (3 or 4) as well as a figure achieving a low score (1 or 2). After verbally specifying with which figure they can identify more strongly, the children are supposed to further differentiate their score (decision between 1 and 2 or 3 and 4, depending on chosen figure). The illustrated figures are adapted on the children’s sex. This questionnaire is available in german and english.

detail.title: Preschool and kindergarten Behaviour Scales, second edition (PKBS‑2)
detail.introduction: The Preschool and Kindergarten Behavior Scales–Second Edition (PKBS-2) is a behavior rating scale designed for use with children ages 3 through 6 years. This unique behavior rating scale is easy to use, very practical, and based on a solid foundation of research. With 76 items on two separate scales, it provides an integrated and functional appraisal of the social skills and problem behaviors of young children. The scales can be completed by a variety of behavioral informants, such as parents, teachers, and other caregivers.

detail.title: Preschool Evaluation Scale (PES‑2)
detail.introduction: The Preschool Evaluation Scale-Second Edition (PES-2) was developed to provide educators, diagnosticians, pediatricians, and psychologists with a measure of child development from 0 through 72 months of age. The PES-2 may be used to contribute to the early identification of students with developmental delays for the purpose of implementing an intervention plan for remediation. The PES-2 is based on the most commonly recognized domains of child development identifi ed in the federal defi nition of developmental delays (PL 99-457). Each subscale is associated with one of the developmental domains.

detail.title: Preschool Numeracy Scales
detail.introduction: The focus of this study was to construct and validate twelve brief early numeracy assessment tasks that measure the skills and concepts identified as key to early mathematics development by the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (2006) and the National Mathematics Advisory Panel (2008)—as well as critical developmental precursors to later mathematics skill by the Common Core State Standards (CCSS; 2010). Participants were 393 preschool children ages 3 to 5 years old. Measure development and validation occurred through three analytic phases designed to ensure that the measures were brief, reliable, and valid. These measures included: one-to-one counting, cardinality, counting subsets, subitizing, number comparison, set comparison, number order, numeral identification, set-to-numerals, story problems, number combinations, and verbal counting.

detail.title: Preschool Self-Regulation Assessment (PSRA)

PSRA offers a "portable" direct assessment of young children's self regulation and is designed to assess self-regulation in emotional, attentional, and behavioral domains by using a brief, structured battery of tasks.

detail.title: Preschool Situational Self-Regulation Toolkit (PRSIST)
detail.introduction: The Preschool Situational Self-Regulation Tool (PRSIST) is an observational assessment of children’s cognitive and behavioural self-regulation. For this assessment, children are engaged in a group activity (i.e., memory card game) and an individual activity (i.e., curiosity boxes guessing game), in which children’s behaviours are rated on key aspects of self-regulation (e.g., was the child self-directed, engaging in the activity with little prompting; did the child control their behaviours and stay within the rules of the activity).

fields.label: Prior qualifications/training required
fields.value: Prior qualifications required include completion of structured PRSIST training; observers were required to meet reliability thresholds, including a mean difference in ratings ≤ 0.75 points, item-level correlations ≥ 0.70, and at least 80% of ratings within one scale point.

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: scoring requires judgment but is supported by detailed behavioral anchors.

fields.label: Availability of guidance
fields.value: structured online training module, detailed item descriptions, developmental anchors, and activity protocols are provided, and training materials are freely available online.

fields.label: Time required
fields.value: Administration time varies by activity: the group memory game lasts approximately 10 minutes, the curiosity boxes activity approximately 5 minutes, and the obstacle course up to 10 minutes; activities are administered across multiple sessions within a single day.

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: Participants were 80 children aged 3 to 5 years (mean age 4.46 years, SD = 0.73; range 3.10 – 5.88) enrolled in seven preschool services in or near a metropolitan city in Australia. The sample included 28 three-year-olds, 31 four-year-olds, and 21 five-year-olds. Children resided predominantly in middle- to high-socioeconomic areas (SEIFA deciles 6 – 8). All children spoke English as a first language and had no formal diagnoses of developmental delay. Recruitment was based on enrolment and consent within participating centres rather than random or stratified sampling, and the sample was not nationally representative.

detail.title: Pupil Behaviour Questionnaire (PBQ)
detail.introduction: The PBQ is a brief, 15-item teacher-report measure that screens behavioural and socio-emotional adjustment in 4–9 year olds to guide early support in school settings.

fields.value: Allwood, Allen, Price, Hayes, Edwards, Ball, Ukoumunne, & Ford

fields.label: Prior qualifications/training required
fields.value: The PBQ was developed for use by classroom teachers and does not require formal clinical or specialist qualifications for completion

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: Scoring involves summing the six item scores to produce a total score ranging from 0 to 12. The scoring process is simple and requires no specialized training.

fields.label: Floor effects
fields.value: In the STARS: Incredible Years evaluation, the authors report that PBQ was administered at baseline and follow-up, but the planned intermediate data collection points were cancelled. The evaluation also notes that teacher turnover affected continuity in PBQ reporting across time points.

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: The UK validation sample consisted of 2,074 children from the STARS trial, with an additional high-risk comparison sample of 41 children from the SKIP study. Teacher-completed PBQ data were available for all 2,074 children in the STARS sample and for 30 of the 41 children in the SKIP sample. Children in the STARS sample were drawn from 80 primary schools in Devon, Plymouth, and Torbay in South West England. The mean age was 6.3 years with a standard deviation of 1.3 years, covering Reception to Year 4, corresponding to ages 4 to 9 years. The sample was balanced by gender with 53 percent boys. The SKIP comparison sample consisted of children aged 5 to 12 years who were at risk of or had experienced school exclusion, with 95 percent of this group being boys. The authors note that the regional sample had lower ethnic diversity than the national UK population

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The PBQ was used in the STARS: Incredible Years® Teacher Classroom Management efficacy trial as the main secondary outcome measure of pupil classroom behaviour. It was administered to Reception pupils at baseline and to the same cohort again at end of Year 2 (ages 6 – 7). The PBQ is a six-item teacher-reported questionnaire, with each item rated on a three-point scale (“never happens”, “occasionally happens”, “frequently happens”), producing a total score range of 0 – 12, where higher scores indicate worse behaviour. It was selected as the main behavioural outcome because it directly captures low-level disruptive behaviours that affect classroom learning, which formed the first link in the programme’s theory of change.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the STARS: Incredible Years evaluation, the authors report that PBQ was administered at baseline and follow-up, but the planned intermediate data collection points were cancelled. The evaluation also notes that teacher turnover affected continuity in PBQ reporting across time points.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: No structural adaptations were made to the PBQ itself. However, data collection was disrupted by COVID-19, and the planned midpoint PBQ assessment in summer 2020 was cancelled. As a result, PBQ data were collected only at baseline and final follow-up (summer 2021). Additionally, due to the cancellation of Key Stage 1 assessments, the PBQ was elevated from a secondary to the main behavioural outcome within the revised analysis plan

fields.label: Source 1
fields.value: Allwood, M., Allen, K., Price, A., Hayes, R., Edwards, V., Ball, S., ... & Ford, T. (2018). The reliability and validity of the pupil behaviour questionnaire: a child classroom behaviour assessment tool. Emotional and Behavioural Difficulties, 23(4), 361-371.

detail.title: Quality Learning Instrument
detail.introduction: The "Quality Learning Instrument" (QLI) is an observation tool used to evaluate the quality of a child's learning experience in early childhood education settings. It assesses the learning environment from the child's perspective by analyzing the interplay between the children's actions, the teaching strategies, and the physical environment. The QLI focuses on key themes like motivation and independence to determine if the learning and developmental needs of the children are being met

detail.title: Qualls Early Learning Inventory (QELI)
detail.introduction: This inventory for grades pre-K through 1 uses teacher ratings of many of the student characteristics that are important for success in the primary grades. It is designed to supplement the achievement information that can be obtained with the Iowa Assessments primary batteries in kindergarten and first grade. Together, the inventory and the achievement battery can provide a comprehensive picture of the strengths a student brings to the classroom and the areas in most need of improvement for enhancing the student's opportunities for growth.The Qualls Early Learning Inventory can provide diagnostic information in six areas: general knowledge, oral communication, written language, math concepts, work habits, and attentive behavior. It allows for an assessment of the student's knowledge and typical behavior in everyday classroom academic and social activities. The inventory can be completed by the teacher in 5-10 minutes, including time for making brief, supplemental written comments.

detail.title: Quantitative Reasoning Assessment
detail.introduction: The Quantitative Reasoning Test assesses young children’s ability to reason about numerical quantities and relations rather than procedural counting skill. It targets four theoretically defined aspects of quantitative reasoning: additive composition, inverse relations between addition and subtraction, additive reasoning, and multiplicative reasoning. The assessment is intended for children at school entry and measures conceptual reasoning about quantities rather than computational fluency.

measures.name: Rapid Automatized Naming and Rapid Alternating Stimulus Tests. (RAN/RAS)

listing.ages: 5 years old, 6 years old, 6+ years old

detail.title: Rapid Automatized Naming and Rapid Alternating Stimulus Tests. (RAN/RAS)
detail.introduction:
The RAN and RAS Tests are considered the “gold standard” of naming tests. They reflect three decades of clinical evidence and research across all parts of the United States, Canada, Europe, Israel, Asia, and Australia that have examined the relation between processing speed and reading. In addition, the tests are simple, fun, and quick to administer, making them important additions to any prediction battery or diagnostic assessment of oral and written language for children and adolescents. It is helpful for identifying students who may be at risk for reading failure.
On all tests the examinee is asked to name each stimulus item as quickly as possible without making any mistakes, such as a letter or color and name. Scores are also based on the amount of time required to name all of the stimulus items on each test. The group of six tests usually take about five to ten minutes to administer, depending on the age, language status (first or second language), and reading abilities of the child. This includes time for directions and practice items per test.

detail.title: Remote Infant Studies of Early Learning (RISE) Battery
detail.introduction: Remote Infant Studies of Early Learning is a battery intended to provide robust looking time measures of cognitive development that can be administered remotely to inform our understanding of individual developmental trajectories in typical and atypical populations, particularly infant siblings of autistic children. This battery was developed to inform our understanding of early cognitive and language development in infants who will later receive a diagnosis of autism. Using tasks that have been successfully implemented in lab-based paradigms, we included assessments of attention, memory, prediction, word recognition, numeracy, multimodal processing, and social evaluation.

detail.title: Renfrew Action Picture Test
detail.introduction: The Renfrew Action Picture Test (RAPT; 5th edition) is a standardised assessment tool widely used by speech and language therapists to evaluate children’s expressive language skills.

fields.label: Proficiencies
fields.value: Expressive vocabulary, Morphology, Grammar, Receptive vocabulary, Syntax, Narrative skills, Inferencing, Language reasoning

fields.label: Floor effects
fields.value: Across both the URLEY and Nuffield Early Language Intervention (NELI) evaluations, the authors report that the Renfrew Action Picture Test was used only as part of a composite language outcome, rather than being analysed as a standalone measure. In both trials, the Information and Grammar subscales contributed to broader expressive language composites alongside other language assessments, and neither evaluation presents separate analyses of RAPT subscales. This indicates that, within these EEF evaluations, RAPT functioned as a complementary component of a wider language battery rather than as an independent outcome measure.

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: The study included 104 foundation-year students aged between 4 years 7 months and 5 years 7 months at school entry, with a mean age of 5 years. Sixty-six percent of the sample was identified as culturally and linguistically diverse. Children were recruited from three low socioeconomic primary schools in Queensland, Australia.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The Renfrew Action Picture Test was used as a standardised outcome measure of expressive language and grammar in multiple EEF evaluations. In the URLEY trial, it contributed to the composite language outcome, alongside the British Picture Vocabulary Scale and CELF, to assess language development in nursery and reception children aged 3 – 5. Both the RAPT Information and RAPT Grammar subscales were included as specific subcomponents of the composite language score. In the Nuffield Early Language Intervention (NELI) evaluation, the Renfrew Action Picture Test was administered to Reception-aged children (4 – 5 years) as part of a broader language assessment battery, with the Information and Grammar subscales contributing to a composite expressive language outcome, rather than being analysed as standalone measures.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: Across both the URLEY and Nuffield Early Language Intervention (NELI) evaluations, the authors report that the Renfrew Action Picture Test was used only as part of a composite language outcome, rather than being analysed as a standalone measure. In both trials, the Information and Grammar subscales contributed to broader expressive language composites alongside other language assessments, and neither evaluation presents separate analyses of RAPT subscales. This indicates that, within these EEF evaluations, RAPT functioned as a complementary component of a wider language battery rather than as an independent outcome measure.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: The authors do not report any structural adaptations to the Renfrew Action Picture Test in either the URLEY or NELI evaluations. However, in both trials, RAPT was used within a composite outcome framework, representing an analytic adaptation that shaped how RAPT data were interpreted. In addition, in NELI, RAPT was administered only at post-test as part of the language battery, rather than at both baseline and follow-up, reflecting an adaptation to the assessment design rather than to the instrument itself.

detail.title: Renfrew Expressive Vocabulary Test (REV)
detail.introduction: The Renfrew Expressive Vocabulary Test (REV) – formerly the Renfrew Word Finding Vocabulary Test – is a quick and easy tool to assess children’s expressive vocabulary. It is designed for children between the ages of 3 years and 11 years and 11 months and is an invaluable resource for Speech and Language Therapists, Special Educational Needs Coordinators, and other professionals engaged with language development.The REV assesses the extent to which pictures of words, arranged in order of difficulty, can be named correctly. Completely revised, this new edition has updated words and images to ensure it reflects the vocabulary of children today and has been expanded to include adjectives and verbs, in addition to nouns.

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The efficacy trial of Talking Time©, an oral language intervention for the early years, uses the REV alongside the Renfrew Action Picture Test (RAPT) to construct a composite standardised index as the primary outcome measure.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the pilot, the test took an average of 7:55 minutes to complete.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: The pilot also revealed that the assessment results were difficult to score without access to a recording on the assessment. It was decided to audio-record all the assessments to allow the assessor to more accurately score the results. This in turn led to the need to obtain parental consents from parents, which had important implications in terms of logistical implementation and sample size.

detail.title: Repetitive Behavior Questionnaire
detail.introduction: The RBQ-3 is a 20-item questionnaire based on the RBQ-2. It is a 20-item evaluation tool that was developed from two existing semi-structured interview measures, the Repetitive Behaviors Interview and the Diagnostic Interview for Social and Communication Disorders. The RBQ-2 broadly measures unusual sensory interests, repetitive motor movements, rigidity/adherence to routine, and preoccupations with restricted patterns of interest.

fields.label: Non-UK standardisation sample
fields.value: The SSBS‑2 norm sample included 2,280 individuals. The norm sample was drawn from the United States and stratified by age, gender, school setting, community and geographic region, race and ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and special education status. Of the 2,280 cases, 1,700 were carried over from the original SSBS norm sample collected between 1990 and 1992, and 580 additional cases were added between 1998 and 2001. The resulting normative data therefore span an 11-year collection period, with most data being at least 10 years old at the time of SSBS‑2 publication in 2002. The final sample included 1,203 males and 1,077 females, indicating an overrepresentation of males. Several demographic groups were either oversampled (e.g., White students, students from the Western U.S., students receiving special education services) or undersampled (e.g., Hispanic students and kindergarten-aged children).

detail.title: Shape School Task
detail.introduction: The Shape School Task is a child-friendly measure of executive functioning that assesses inhibitory control and cognitive flexibility. Children are shown cartoon figures varying in shape, colour, and facial expression, and are asked to name the colour or shape according to different rules. In some conditions they must inhibit responses (e.g., not naming sad figures), while in others they must switch between naming colour or shape depending on cues (e.g., whether the figure is wearing a hat).

detail.title: Social, Academic, and Emotional Behavior Risk Screener –Teacher rating scale (SAEBRS-TRS)
detail.introduction: The SAEBRS (Social, Academic, and Emotional Behavior Risk Screener) is a brief, norm-referenced tool for screening all students to identify those who are at risk for social-emotional behavior (SEB) problems. SAEBRS is one of the only SEB universal screening tools built to assess both the absence of problem behaviors and symptomatology (e.g., internalizing and externalizing behaviors) and the presence of well-being and competencies (e.g., social-emotional skills).

detail.title: Social Competence and Behavior Evaluation scale — Short Form (SCBE-30)
detail.introduction: The SCBE-30 (Social Competence and Behavior Evaluation Scale, Short Form) is a widely used 30-item questionnaire, often completed by teachers, to assess social skills and behavioral patterns (anxiety, aggression, prosociality) in young children (ages 3-6). It helps understand a child's adjustment, identifying strengths and weaknesses in emotional regulation and social interaction, with scales for Social Competence (SC), Anger/Aggression (AA), and Anxiety/Withdrawal (AW).

Participants were recruited from 12 school research sites in 8 U.S. states (California, Colorado, Georgia, Hawaii, Illinois, Iowa, North Carolina, and Massachusetts), representing all four U.S. geographic regions. Children were distributed across grades K – 12, with 55% in grades K – 6 and 45% in grades 7 – 12. The sample was 51.2% male and 48.8% female. detail.title: Social – Emotional Assets and Resilience scales – Teacher (SEARS‑T).
detail.introduction:
A Strengths-Based Tool to Evaluate Social–Emotional Assets, Resiliencies, and Competencies in Children and Adolescents
Focusing on a child’s strengths, the SEARS can be used with children and adolescents who exhibit a variety of clinical problems or who are at high risk for developing such problems.The SEARS comprises a cross-informant system for measuring social-emotional competencies such as friendship skills, empathy, interpersonal skills, social support, problem solving, emotional competence, social maturity, self-concept, self-management, social independence, cognitive strategies, and resilience. Higher item, scale, and total scores are always indicative of perceptions of higher levels of social-emotional competence. Useful when working within MTSS (Multi-Tiered Systems of Support) and RTI (Response to Intervention) frameworks.

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: For the development of the SEARS‑T long form, 418 teachers provided behavioral ratings on a total of 1,673 K – 12 students in public and private school systems throughout the United States (Merrell, Cohn & Tom, 2011). Of this sample, 380 teachers (rating 1,524 students) participated in a national norming study for the teacher rater form of the SEARS system. Within the final sample of teacher raters, approximately 26 % were male, 72 % were general education teachers, 7 % were special education teachers, 11 %, were from other settings (e.g., reading programs, gifted programs), 5 % were in nonteaching, student support roles, and 3 % were categorized as ‘other’ (Merrell, Cohn, et al., 2011). The number of years of prior experience for each rater ranged from0 to 50 with a mean of 15. The raters were recruited from 23 participating schoolresearch sites in 10 U.S. states, including California, Colorado, Georgia, Hawaii,Illinois, Iowa, North Carolina, Washington, Oregon, and Massachusetts (Merrell,Cohn, et al., 2011).The children and adolescents for whom SEARS‑T ratings were completed were spread across the K – 12 grade range, with approximately 56 % in the K – 6 grade range, and 44 % in the 7 – 12 grade level. Approximately 49 % of the sample were male, 18 % were identifi ed by their teacher rater as having a disability for purposes of special education service eligibility, 49 % were identifi ed as White/Caucasian, 19 % as African American, 19 % as Hispanic/Latino, 8 % as Asian/Pacifi c Islander, 3 % as Multiracial, 1 % as other, and 0.2 % as Native American (Merrell, Cohn, et al., 2011).

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) has been used across multiple EEF evaluations as a teacher-reported measure of children’s socio-emotional behaviour. In the STARS: Incredible Years evaluation, the teacher version (SDQ‑T) was administered to assess behavioural outcomes for primary-aged pupils at follow-up. In the Tips by Text evaluation, SDQ‑T was used as a secondary outcome measure to capture children’s socio-emotional development, with data collected from teachers at endline. In the Hanen Learning Language and Loving It (LLLI) evaluation, SDQ‑T was administered at endline only to measure socio-emotional behaviour among nursery-aged children (3 – 4 years), with questionnaires completed by setting staff who knew the children well.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: Across the STARS, Tips by Text, and Hanen LLLI evaluations, the authors report limited variation in SDQ‑T scores, with many children scoring at the lower end of the Total Difficulties Score distribution. In the Hanen LLLI trial specifically, SDQ‑T was collected only at post-test and showed little differentiation between pupils, indicating constrained score spread within the nursery sample. Across evaluations, low response rates and missing teacher questionnaires further limited the completeness of SDQ‑T data.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: In the STARS trial, the SDQ remained unchanged as a measure, but its planned longitudinal use was disrupted by COVID-19, with data collected only at the second-year endpoint rather than at multiple time points. In the Tips by Text trial, the SDQ was adapted procedurally from its original design as a paper-based teacher measure in Reception to an online teacher-reported measure in Year 1, reflecting delays caused by school closures. No structural changes to SDQ items or scoring were reported in either study. In the Hanen LLLI evaluation, SDQ‑T was administered only at endline, with no baseline SDQ data collected, reflecting an adaptation to the evaluation design rather than the instrument itself. In addition, SDQ‑T data collection relied on setting staff rather than independent assessors, consistent with standard SDQ guidance but differing from other assessor-led outcome measures used in the same trials. No structural adaptations to the SDQ instrument were reported across the evaluations.

fields.label: Source 1
fields.value: Croft, S., Stride, C., Maughan, B., & Rowe, R. (2015). Validity of the strengths and difficulties questionnaire in preschool-aged children. Pediatrics, 135(5), e1210-e1219.

detail.title: Strong Narrative Assessment Procedure (SNAP)
detail.introduction: The Strong Narrative Assessment Procedure (SNAP; Strong 1998) is an individually administered criterion-based method to measure various skills related to narrative discourse. Children from kindergarten to 8th grade are the appropriate candidates to be administered the SNAP. The SNAP assessment is divided into multiple steps; children recall relevant details of stories, summarize the stories, and answer questions that assess comprehension of the stories following specific instructions. Flexibility in transitioning between verbal and written language is required by students who are administered the SNAP. The ultimate goal of this assessment is to provide an approach to treatment that will support children when engaging in positive social interactions.

detail.introduction: The Stroop Color–Object task extends the classic color-word Stroop effect by using pictures of objects instead of written words, extending the tool to younger children. fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The STRS‑R was used in the STARS: Incredible Years® Teacher Classroom Management efficacy trial as a secondary pupil-level outcome measure to assess teacher – pupil relationships. It was administered to Year 1 – Year 2 pupils (ages 5 – 7) across 139 primary schools in England. The revised version was used only at endpoint (end of Year 2), with baseline behaviour (PBQ) used as the covariate instead of a baseline STRS score. The revised scale consisted of 15 items, scored on a five-point Likert scale, producing a total score range of 25 – 75, with higher scores indicating a more positive teacher – pupil relationship. The scale measured closeness, conflict, and dependency.

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the STARS: Incredible Years evaluation, the authors report that STRS‑R was administered as a teacher-reported questionnaire at a single follow-up time point. The evaluation notes low response rates and challenges related to teacher turnover, which affected the completeness and consistency of STRS‑R data.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: The STRS was formally adapted for the UK context prior to use in the trial. Following internal review, some original STRS items were judged inappropriate in wording and emphasis for UK classrooms, and a revised 15-item version was jointly developed by NFER and the University of Exeter team. The adapted version underwent pilot validation with 247 UK teachers, who completed ratings for one pupil with a strong relationship and one with a strained relationship. This testing demonstrated good external and discriminant validity. Several items were negatively worded and reverse-scored, but no further changes to the scale structure or scoring were made during the trial itself.

detail.title: Sustained Shared Thinking and Emotional Well-being (SSTEW) Scale
detail.introduction: The SSTEW scale is an observational quality rating tool focusing on process quality—in particular, the nature of adult–child interactions that foster sustained shared thinking (i.e. co-constructing thinking, reasoning, scaffolding) as well as emotional well-being / relational pedagogy in early childhood settings.

fields.value: Data were collected in 45 Australian early childhood centres from 669 children aged 3.10 – 5.69 years. The sample consisted of preschool classrooms in urban and regional Australian centres, spanning diverse socioeconomic backgrounds (SEIFA deciles 1 – 8), and including long-day care and preschool services.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: The SSTEW scale was used in the URLEY trial as part of a composite measure of classroom provision quality, alongside ECERS‑3 and ECERS‑E. It was applied in nursery and reception classrooms (ages 3 – 5) to assess the quality of pedagogy, interactions, emotional wellbeing, shared thinking, self-regulation, and communication. Observations were conducted using a seven-point rating scale, and SSTEW scores contributed both to a composite environment rating outcome and were also reported separately at total-scale level.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: No structural adaptations were made to the SSTEW scale itself. However, for analytic purposes, one SSTEW item (“Assessing Language Development”) was removed from the composite provision quality score, as later delivery guidance judged it to focus more on assessment processes than on interactional classroom quality. This adjustment did not materially change the pattern of results. SSTEW observations were conducted by trained observers who were blind to trial allocation, maintaining standardisation of administration.

detail.title: Test of Early Mathematics Ability (TEMA‑3)
detail.introduction: The TEMA-3 measures the mathematics performance of children between the ages of 3-0 and 8-11 and is also useful with older children who have learning problems in mathematics. It can be used as a norm-referenced measure or as a diagnostic instrument to determine specific strengths and weaknesses. Thus, the test can be used to measure progress, evaluate programs, screen for readiness, discover the bases for poor school performance in mathematics, identify gifted students, and guide instruction and remediation. The test measures informal and formal (school-taught) concepts and skills in the following domains: numbering skills, number-comparison facility, numeral literacy, mastery of number facts, calculation skills, and understanding of concepts. It has two parallel forms, each containing 72 items.

detail.title: Test of Early Reading Ability, 4th edition (TERA‑4)
detail.introduction: The Test of Early Reading Ability-Fourth Edition (TERA-4) is a direct measure of reading ability in children ages 4-0 through 8-11. Rather than assessing children's "readiness" for reading, the TERA-4 assesses their mastery of early-developing reading skills. The test has three subtests: Alphabet (measures knowledge of the alphabet and its uses), Conventions (measures knowledge of the conventions of print), and Meaning (measures comprehension of print). A composite, called the General Reading Index, represents overall reading ability.

detail.introduction: The TOLD-P:5 assesses spoken language in young children. It is well constructed, reliable, practical, research-based, and theoretically sound. Professionals can use the TOLD-P:5 to (1) identify children who are significantly below their peers in oral language proficiency, (2) determine their specific strengths and weaknesses in oral language skills, (3) document their progress in remedial programs, and (4) measure oral language in research studies.

detail.title: Test of Preschool Early Literacy (TOPEL)
detail.introduction: Children entering kindergarten or first grade are expected to have sufficient knowledge of vocabulary, phonological awareness, and print knowledge. The Test of Preschool Early Literacy (TOPEL) is a theoretically sound instrument designed to identify preschoolers who are at risk for literacy problems; therefore, allowing early intervention. It is easy to administer; early childhood educators, special educators, psychologists, diagnosticians, and other professionals who are interested in examine skills related to early literacy can administer the test.

detail.title: Test of Word Finding, third edition (TWF‑3)
detail.introduction: The Test of Word Finding, Third Edition (TWF-3) is a norm-referenced, single-word expressive language test that measures a child’s word finding ability. It can be used to identify students who have word finding difficulties, plan intervention, and conduct research. This edition features all new normative data that includes students previously diagnosed with word finding difficulties. In addition, it incorporates new noun and verb target words

detail.introduction: The CMA assesses informal mathematics knowledge in preschool children using 15 tasks involving manipulatives across number, arithmetic, measurement, geometry, spatial relations, and patterning. The tasks reflect developmental mathematics content targeted in pre-kindergarten instruction.

detail.title: The Early Arithmetic, Reading, and Learning Indicators (EARLI)
detail.introduction: The Early Arithmetic, Reading, and Learning Indicators (EARLI) is a set of brief, progress-monitoring measures designed to assess key early literacy and numeracy skills in preschoolers. The assessments measure skills like letter knowledge, expressive vocabulary, and number naming, and track children's development over time.

fields.label: Prior qualifications/training required
fields.value: Expert judgement is required to reliably identify specific behavioral codes in realtime

fields.label: Ease of scoring
fields.value: Moderate.Scores are calculated as rates per minute or weighted scores for specific skill sets (Joint Attention, Social Communication). Data is typically entered into the IGDI online data system for automated reporting.

fields.label: Availability of guidance
fields.value: Available online. Training costs apply for required certification training.

fields.label: Cost
fields.value: No cost to use the system after training completion.

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: The measure was developed and validated in the United States. Infants and toddlers (n = 716) served in one large early childhood program in a large Midwestern city were assessed with the ESI between 2013 and 2018. Because the ESI was adopted by the program as a standard practice, informed consent was not required. The mean age of children at first ESI was 17.0 (SD = 10.0) months, ranging from 4 to 44; however, only children aged 6 to 36 months were included in analyses. Forty-nine percent (n = 351)were female. Eighty-six (12%) children had an IFSP. Home languages were English (n = 344, 48%), Spanish (n = 308, 43%), and Other (n = 64, 9%, for example, Chinese and Arabic).

fields.value: Carta, J.J., Greenwood, C.R., Luze, G.J., Cline, G. and Kuntz, S., 2004. Developing a general outcome measure of growth in social skills for infants and toddlers. Journal of early intervention, 26(2), pp.91-114.

detail.title: The Movement Environment Rating Scale (MOVERS)
detail.introduction:
The Movement Environment Rating Scale (MOVERS) offers a method of measuring the quality of environment and pedagogy in which young children are encouraged to move and be physically active. MOVERS has four sub-scales:
- curriculum, environment and resources for physical development
- pedagogy for physical development
- supporting physical activity and critical thinking
- parents/carers and staff.

detail.title: The Multidimensional assessment of Parenting scale (MAPS)
detail.introduction: The Multidimensional Assessment of Parenting Scale assesses positive and negative parenting practices. The MAPS was developed from established measures of parenting practices to select optimal parenting items constituting both positive and negative dimensions of warmth/hostility and behavioral control appropriate for parents of children across the developmental span from young childhood through adolescence.

fields.value: Scoring is straightforward, summing subscales and computing composite scores based on published scoring rules. Software is not required.

fields.label: Availability of guidance
fields.value: The article provides scoring instructions and model structure; full scoring details are available in the measure documentation upon request. Guidance is available but not proprietary.

fields.label: Validation sample
fields.value: The revised MAPS was validated with 1,699 U.S. parents of children aged 5 to 12. The sample consisted of 45.3% White parents, 25.6% Black parents, 21.2% Hispanic/Latino parents, and 7.9% Asian, multiracial, or other groups. Participants resided across multiple regions, and socioeconomic variability was present across parental education and income levels. The sample showed demographic diversity and was screened through quota sampling to ensure racial and ethnic representation. Although not nationally normed for prevalence estimates, the sampling strategy and sample size yield evidence that exceeds minimal representativeness standards for research validation, but remains non-normative for population comparison

detail.title: The Ounce Scale
detail.introduction: The Ounce Scale is an ongoing, functional assessment for children from birth-42 months (i.e., 3 years, 6 months). It focuses the professional's attention on developmentally significant events in children's lives. It involves families in assessment and provides standards for infant and toddler behavior and development. Unlike other infant/toddler assessments, The Ounce Scale focuses on how children use skills in the context of their natural environment. Professionals and families work together to learn about the child's development in four basic domains: Social and Emotional Development, Communication and Language, Cognitive Development, and Physical Development.

detail.introduction: The Test of Narrative Retell (TNR) is a standardized assessment that evaluates a person's ability to retell a story they have heard, which serves as an indicator of their language skills. It is one of the subtests within the broader Narrative Language Measures (NLM) and measures comprehension, memory, and expressive language through the act of recalling and retelling a narrative

detail.title: The Test of Pragmatic Language (TOPL‑2)
detail.introduction: The Test of Pragmatic Language-2 (TOPL-2) expands on the original for an even more in-depth and comprehensive analysis of social communication in context. The TOPL-2 allows you to assess the effectiveness, and appropriateness, of a student's pragmatic language skills. Administered in approximately 45-60 minutes, it tests six core subcomponents of pragmatic language: physical setting, audience, topic, purpose (speech acts), visual-gestural cues, and abstraction.

detail.title: Theory of Mind (ToM) Battery
detail.introduction: This is a widely-used developmental scale consisting of 5-7 tasks that assess a child's understanding of mental states. The tasks are presented in a specific order of difficulty: Diverse Desires, Diverse Beliefs, Knowledge Access, False Belief, and Hidden Emotion. It is used to measure a child's progression in Theory of Mind development.

detail.title: Torrance tests of Creative Thinking-Figural (TTCT‑F)
detail.introduction: The Figural TTCT uses three picture-based exercises to assess five mental characteristics: • fluency • elaboration • originality • resistance to premature closure • abstractness of titles. Streamlined scoring provides standardized scores for the mental characteristics listed above as well as for the following creative strengths: • emotional expressiveness • unusual visualization • internal visualization • storytelling articulateness • extending or breaking boundaries • movement or action

detail.title: Verbal Behavior Milestones Assessment and Placement Program (VB-MAPP)
detail.introduction: The VB-MAPP gives educators and parents an effective way to assess the learning, language, and social skills of children with autism or other developmental disabilities. Based on established developmental milestones and behavior analysis, the VB-MAPP is a criterion-referenced assessment tool, curriculum guide, and skill-tracking system. It provides a clear and accurate picture of the whole child, identifying barriers that impede learning and informing IEP development.

detail.title: York Assessment for Reading Comprehension (YARC)
detail.introduction: The York Assessment of Reading for Comprehension (YARC) is a standardized, one-to-one diagnostic reading assessment for children aged 4–7 (early years) that evaluates their phonological skills, word reading, and text comprehension. It provides a detailed profile of a student's reading abilities, identifying strengths and weaknesses to inform appropriate educational interventions and support

The evaluation notes that the assessor-led nature of YARC required trained staff and sufficient testing time, which affected data completeness under disrupted conditions.

sections.heading: Insight from EEF Early Years Trials

fields.label: Description of use(s)
fields.value: In the Tips by Text randomised controlled trial, YARC was used as the primary literacy outcome measure to assess children’s reading comprehension skills. The intervention targeted children in Reception year (ages 4 – 5), with follow-up extending into Year 1 (ages 5 – 6) due to COVID-related delays. Parents were randomised at the individual level, and YARC was administered at post-test to evaluate the impact of parent texting on literacy outcomes In the Nuffield Early Language Intervention (NELI) effectiveness trial, YARC was used as a secondary outcome measure, specifically the YARC Early Word Reading test, to assess early reading outcomes alongside primary language measures. The trial involved Reception-aged children (4 – 5 years) receiving a 20-week structured oral language intervention delivered by trained teaching assistants In the Flexible Phonics trial, reading comprehension was assessed as a secondary outcome, alongside early word recognition and mispronunciation correction. The report confirms that reading comprehension was formally tested pre- and post-intervention in Reception children aged 4 – 5, although the specific reading comprehension instrument is not explicitly named as YARC in this report. Therefore, this document cannot be used as a confirmed source of YARC usage

fields.label: Key Learnings
fields.value: In the Tips by Text evaluation, the authors report that YARC was administered only at follow-up and that disruptions to testing schedules led to high attrition and incomplete outcome data. The evaluation notes that the assessor-led nature of YARC required trained staff and sufficient testing time, which affected data completeness under disrupted conditions.

fields.label: Adaptations made
fields.value: In the Tips by Text trial, major procedural adaptations occurred due to COVID-19. The intervention was extended from 9 months to 12 months, and post-testing using YARC was postponed and partially cancelled, resulting in substantial attrition in outcome data. These adaptations affected testing timing and sample size, not the structure of YARC itself In the NELI trial, YARC was used strictly as a secondary outcome tool, alongside LanguageScreen and multiple language measures. There is no evidence of any adaptation to YARC’s format, administration, or scoring in this evaluation. The only adjustment was its position as a supplementary rather than primary measure The Flexible Phonics report documents adaptations to training delivery (online instead of in-person), shortened intervention duration, and school closures due to COVID-19, but no adaptation to any named reading comprehension assessment is reported,
